meta.blurb: Look up from a dark hilltop and you are looking into the past. In fifty short steps, this book follows the story back to the Big Bang and forward to the far future, and says plainly what nobody knows yet.
meta.bible:
You: the reader, sitting on a hilltop on a clear night; the book begins and ends there. Universe, Milky Way, Sun, Earth, Moon, Jupiter, Mars, Andromeda: real places. Nicolaus Copernicus (1543, the Sun at the centre), Galileo (1610, four moons of Jupiter), Isaac Newton (late 1600s, Gravity) and Albert Einstein (1915, general Relativity): real scientists, told plainly. Key terms: Light-year, Galaxy, Galaxies, Telescope, Black Hole, Event Horizon, Big Bang, Redshift, Hydrogen, Helium, Carbon, Oxygen, Iron, Calcium, Nuclear Fusion, Microwave, Inflation, Supernova, Red Giant, White Dwarf, Electrons, Protons, Neutrons, Quarks, Quantum, Electromagnetism, String, Dark Matter, Dark Energy, Big Rip, Gravitational Waves, Observable. Facts: the Sun's light takes about eight minutes to reach the Earth; the Milky Way holds at least a hundred billion stars; the universe is about 13.8 billion years old; the solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago; the microwave glow dates from about 380,000 years after the beginning; the Sun will swell into a red giant in about five billion years; ordinary matter is about 5 per cent of the universe, dark matter about a quarter and dark energy about two thirds; the observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across. Where science is unsure (what came before the Big Bang, inflation, dark matter, dark energy, how life began, the far future), the text says so plainly. Voice and tone: wondering, calm and honest, speaking to you directly, with fresh everyday comparisons (dough and raisins, a cooling cup of tea, a marble in a bowl); no named people other than the historical scientists above. FULL-LENGTH ADDITIONS (200 beats, twenty chapters). Chapter 1: Proxima Centauri, the nearest star after the Sun, a little over four light-years away; the Moon is about 384,000 kilometres from the Earth and its light takes about a second and a quarter to arrive; light travels about 300,000 kilometres a second; Constellations, Planets, Venus, Saturn, Sirius, Orion: real names.
Chapter 2: the Sun holds nearly all the mass of the solar system and about 1,300,000 Earths would fit inside it; the eight planets in order are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune; Venus is the hottest planet, about 465 degrees; Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a huge storm; Neptune was found in 1846 by calculation; Pluto is a Dwarf planet; Halley's Comet returns about every 76 years; the Kuiper Belt and the Asteroid Belt are real; Voyager 1 was launched in 1977 and is the farthest human-made object, more than twenty billion kilometres away; Asteroids, Comets, Rovers, Rings.
Chapter 3: stars are blue when hot, yellow-white like the Sun, red when cool; Betelgeuse is a red giant in Orion, wide enough to swallow the orbits of the inner planets; red dwarfs are about three stars in four; the Milky Way is a flat spiral about 100,000 light-years across, the Sun lies about 26,000 light-years from the centre and circles it once in about 230 million years; the Orion Nebula is a Nebula about 1,300 light-years away where stars are born; Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away and is the farthest thing the eye alone can see; the Magellanic Clouds are small galaxies near the Milky Way; Spiral, Elliptical, Irregular, Local Group, Cluster, Void; in 1995 the Hubble Space Telescope stared for about ten days at a patch of sky as small as a grain of sand at arm's length and found about 3,000 galaxies, the Hubble Deep Field; Hubble, Cosmic Web, Filaments.
Chapter 4 (real history, told plainly): Aristotle (4th century BC) argued the Earth is round from its curved shadow on the Moon in an eclipse; Eratosthenes (about 240 BC) estimated the size of the Earth by comparing shadows at Syene and Alexandria and got close to the true figure of about 40,000 kilometres around; Aristarchus of Samos (about 270 BC) suggested the Sun is at the centre but few agreed; Ptolemy (about 150 AD) built an Earth-centred system with circles on circles called Epicycles that predicted the planets well for about 1,400 years; Copernicus, a Polish astronomer, published his Sun-centred book in 1543; Tycho Brahe made careful measurements by eye; Johannes Kepler (1609) showed planets move on ovals called Ellipses, faster when nearer the Sun; Galileo in 1610 saw mountains on the Moon, four moons of Jupiter and the phases of Venus, and in 1633 was forced by the Church to take back his claim and lived under house arrest; Retrograde means a planet seems to move backwards for a while; the Inquisition was the Church court.
Chapter 5 (real history and physics): Isaac Newton published his Principia in 1687; by a famous story an apple set him thinking, and his cannonball thought experiment shows an object thrown fast enough would fall right around the Earth; his law: every object pulls every other, more for heavier objects and less with distance, so doubling the distance makes the pull four times weaker; Edmond Halley used it to predict the comet's return in 1758, after Halley had died; Mercury's orbit turned slightly more than Newton's law gave; Einstein's Special Relativity (1905) says light has the same speed for every observer and moving clocks run slower; his General Relativity (1915) says mass bends Space-time and objects follow the curves; in 1919 Arthur Eddington's expeditions (one on the island of Principe) saw starlight bend near the Sun during an eclipse; Gravitational lensing is where a galaxy bends light from far behind it into arcs and rings; GPS satellites have clocks that run a little fast compared with the ground and must be corrected or errors would reach kilometres in a day; Spacetime, Eclipse, Orbit.
Chapter 6: a star is a balance between gravity pulling in and heat pushing out; the speed needed to escape the Earth is about eleven kilometres a second; John Michell in 1783 imagined stars whose gravity would trap even light; a black hole forms when a very heavy star's core collapses; if the Sun became a black hole it would be only about six kilometres across and the Earth would keep orbiting as before; the Event Horizon is the point of no return and is not a solid surface; Cygnus X-1 was the first strong black hole candidate, found by the X-rays of hot gas; supermassive black holes sit at the centre of most large galaxies; Sagittarius A* at the centre of the Milky Way weighs about four million Suns, shown by years of tracking stars that orbit it; in 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope, a network of radio dishes across the Earth, made the first picture of the shadow of a black hole, in the galaxy Messier 87, about 55 million light-years away; Singularity is the point where the theory gives nonsense; theory suggests black holes slowly lose energy and shrink over unimaginably long times, never yet seen.
Chapter 7 (real history): until the 1920s many astronomers thought the Milky Way was the whole universe; Henrietta Leavitt (about 1912, Harvard) found that bright pulsing stars called Cepheids pulse more slowly the brighter they are, which gives a measuring stick for distance; Edwin Hubble in 1924 used a Cepheid to show that Andromeda lies far outside the Milky Way; Vesto Slipher in the 1910s found that the light of most spiral nebulae is shifted to red; the Doppler effect is why an ambulance siren drops in pitch as it passes, and Redshift is light stretched to longer, redder waves; Georges Lemaitre, a Belgian priest and physicist, worked out in 1927 that the universe must be expanding, and Hubble's 1929 measurements showed that farther galaxies run away faster; every galaxy sees the others moving away, so there is no centre; Einstein had added a Cosmological constant to keep the universe still and dropped it when expansion was found; galaxies, planets and atoms do not expand because gravity and other forces hold them together; Andromeda is moving towards the Milky Way; the Hubble constant is about twenty kilometres a second faster for each million light-years, and two methods of measuring it give slightly different answers, an open puzzle called the Hubble tension; Cepheids, Spiral nebulae, Balloon.
Raisins, Dough.
Chapter 8: nearly fourteen billion years ago the universe was extremely hot and dense; the name Big Bang was coined by the astronomer Fred Hoyle in a radio talk in 1949, and it stuck; Quarks and Gluons made a hot soup, and at about a millionth of a second the quarks gathered into Protons and Neutrons; Antimatter: every particle has a partner that destroys it, and a tiny surplus of matter, about one part in a billion, survived for reasons nobody knows; within the first few minutes protons and neutrons joined into Helium and a little Lithium, leaving about three quarters Hydrogen and one quarter helium by mass, a mix that calculations of the 1940s predicted and the oldest gas clouds confirm; for about 380,000 years the universe was a glowing Plasma fog; Inflation is the idea of a huge growth in a tiny fraction of a second, a leading but unproved idea that would explain why the universe is so smooth and why galaxies grew from tiny seeds.
Chapter 9: at about 380,000 years the universe cooled to about 3,000 degrees, electrons joined nuclei to make the first atoms and light was set free; that light, the Cosmic microwave background, has been stretched by the expansion into microwaves and is now about 270 degrees below zero; Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, at Bell Laboratories in New Jersey in 1964 and 1965, found an unexplained hiss in a horn antenna that came from every direction and persisted after they cleaned out the pigeon droppings; they won the Nobel Prize in 1978; a small part of the static on old television sets between channels came from the Big Bang; satellites COBE, WMAP and Planck mapped the glow and found ripples of about one part in 100,000; denser patches pulled in more matter by gravity and grew into galaxies; the Dark ages lasted for hundreds of millions of years with no stars; the first stars switched on a few hundred million years after the beginning, were huge, hot and blue and short-lived, and have not been seen directly; their light broke hydrogen atoms apart in an era called Reionisation; the James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, sees infrared light and has found galaxies from less than 400 million years after the beginning, some surprisingly bright and large; Microwaves, Infrared.
Chapter 10: a star is born when a gas cloud collapses and its core reaches about ten million degrees so that hydrogen cores fuse; the core of the Sun is about 15 million degrees; Nuclear fusion turns four hydrogen cores into one helium core and a little mass into energy, as in E=mc2, and the Sun turns about four million tonnes of mass into energy every second; light made in the core takes many thousands of years to work its way out to the surface of the Sun; the Sun is about halfway through a lifetime of about ten billion years; heavy stars live only millions of years while the smallest red dwarfs may shine for trillions of years; in giant stars helium fuses into Carbon and Oxygen, and in the heaviest stars the layers go on up to Iron, which gives no energy when it fuses; a Supernova is the explosion of a heavy star, as bright as a whole galaxy for weeks; Chinese astronomers recorded a guest star in the year 1054 and its remains are the Crab Nebula; a Neutron star is the collapsed core, as small as a city, and a teaspoon of it would weigh about two billion tonnes; a Pulsar is a spinning neutron star that flashes; in 2017 a collision of two neutron stars was seen in gravitational waves and in light, and such collisions make much of the gold and other heavy elements; Protostar, Gold, Platinum.
Chapter 11: the body is mostly Oxygen, Carbon, Hydrogen and Nitrogen; the hydrogen came from the Big Bang and nearly everything else from stars; the solar system formed about 4,600 million years ago from a collapsing cloud, perhaps nudged by a nearby exploding star; the spinning cloud flattened into a Disc, the Sun formed in the middle, and dust stuck into pebbles, rocks and Planetesimals that grew into planets over tens of millions of years; rocky planets formed near the Sun and gas giants beyond the Frost line where ice could exist; the young Earth was molten and its heavy iron sank to make the core; most scientists think the Moon formed when a body about the size of Mars, called Theia, hit the young Earth and the debris gathered into the Moon; the origin of Earth's water is debated, some from its own rocks and some perhaps from asteroids and comets; the Moon causes tides, helps keep Earth's tilt steady and drifts away by about four centimetres a year; Earth's iron core makes a Magnetic field that shields the air from the solar wind; Earth lies in the Habitable zone where liquid water can exist; the Earth is about four and a half billion years old.
Chapter 12 (science is unsure how life began; the text says so): the oldest signs of life are more than 3,500 million years old, such as layered rock structures called Stromatolites made by Microbes; Stanley Miller and Harold Urey in 1952 sent sparks through a flask of simple gases and water and made Amino acids, the building blocks of proteins; the Murchison meteorite fell in Australia in 1969 and held amino acids; ideas for where life began include warm pools, hot springs on the sea floor called hydrothermal vents (found in 1977) and clay; the RNA world idea says RNA, which can store information and speed up reactions, may have come first; for about two billion years life was only tiny single cells; Photosynthesis released oxygen and about 2,400 million years ago the Great Oxidation changed the air; complex cells with a nucleus appeared about two billion years ago and Mitochondria may be swallowed bacteria; animals appeared about 600 million years ago; Charles Darwin published Natural selection in 1859; all life shares the DNA code; an asteroid ended the dinosaurs about 66 million years ago; our species Homo sapiens is about 300,000 years old, so if Earth's history were one day we would appear in the last six seconds.
Chapter 13: before 1995 no planet was known around an ordinary star like the Sun; Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found 51 Pegasi b in 1995 and won the Nobel Prize in 2019; Exoplanets are planets of other stars; the Kepler Space Telescope (launched 2009) found planets by the tiny dimming of a star as a planet crosses in front of it, called a Transit; more than 5,000 exoplanets are confirmed and astronomers think most stars have planets, so the Milky Way holds billions; some planets have two suns, Hot Jupiters orbit very close to their stars, and Super-Earths between Earth and Neptune in size are common; Proxima b orbits Proxima Centauri in its habitable zone (found 2016); TRAPPIST-1 is a small star about 40 light-years away with seven rocky planets, several in the habitable zone, but nobody knows if any can support life; the James Webb Space Telescope studies the air of other planets by the starlight that passes through it, and Biosignatures are gases that might hint at life, none yet confirmed; Mars once had water; Europa (a moon of Jupiter) and Enceladus (a moon of Saturn) have oceans of liquid water under ice, and Cassini flew through the geysers of Enceladus; Titan has lakes of methane; nothing alive has been found beyond the Earth; SETI is the search for radio signals from other civilisations, begun by Frank Drake in 1960; the Wow signal of 1977 was a strong radio burst lasting 72 seconds that never repeated; the Fermi question asks why, if the galaxy is old and full of planets, we have not met anyone; the two Voyager probes carry Golden Records with greetings in 55 languages, music and sounds of the Earth.
Chapter 14: four forces: Gravity (weakest, but it always adds up and reaches everywhere), Electromagnetism (electricity, magnetism and light; it holds atoms together and drives all of chemistry; radio waves, microwaves, visible light and X-rays are all the same kind of wave), the Strong force (holds the cores of atoms together) and the Weak force (causes some radioactivity and makes fusion in the Sun possible); a small magnet can lift a paper clip against the pull of the whole Earth; an atom is about 100,000 times wider than its nucleus, so it is almost all empty space; Protons and neutrons are made of three Quarks each; Electrons; Neutrinos barely interact, and tens of billions from the Sun pass through your thumbnail every second; Max Planck in 1900 found that energy comes in small packets called Quanta; Einstein in 1905 showed light comes in packets called Photons; in the Double slit experiment electrons sent one at a time build up a wave pattern, as if each went through both slits; quantum theory predicts only chances, and Einstein was uneasy about this; Werner Heisenberg in 1927 stated the Uncertainty principle: we cannot know exactly both where a particle is and how it moves, and this is part of nature and not a flaw of instruments; quantum physics gave us lasers, transistors, computers, LEDs and MRI scanners and is one of the most precisely tested theories ever, yet scientists still disagree about what it means.
Chapter 15: the Standard model lists all the known particles and three of the four forces and matches experiments superbly; the Higgs boson was found in 2012 at CERN, whose Large Hadron Collider is a ring 27 kilometres round near Geneva, and the Higgs field is how particles get their mass; the Standard Model leaves out gravity, dark matter and dark energy and cannot say why matter beat antimatter; general relativity describes the huge and quantum physics the tiny and they do not fit together; they clash at the centres of black holes and at the beginning of the universe, where gravity and quantum effects both matter; the Planck length is about a hundred billion billion times smaller than a proton; Einstein spent his last decades looking for a single unified theory and did not find it; String theory says particles are tiny vibrating strings and needs extra dimensions; Loop quantum gravity says space itself is made of tiny grains; neither has been tested, because the energies needed are far beyond any machine we can build; LIGO detected gravitational waves for the first time in 2015 from two black holes, about 36 and 29 times the mass of the Sun, that merged about 1.3 billion light-years away, and the ripple moved the 4-kilometre arms of the detector by much less than the width of a proton; Collider, Particles.
Chapter 16: Fritz Zwicky in the 1930s noticed that galaxies in a cluster move too fast for the visible matter to hold them; Vera Rubin in the 1970s measured how fast stars far out in galaxies orbit and found they go as fast as those near the middle, so each galaxy must hold much unseen mass; Dark matter gives out no light and is felt only through gravity, and there is about five times as much of it as ordinary matter; more evidence comes from gravitational lensing and from the Bullet Cluster, two galaxy clusters that collided and whose gas was slowed while most of the mass passed straight through; the particles of dark matter are unknown, detectors deep underground have not caught one, and a few scientists try to change the law of gravity instead; computer simulations with dark matter grow a cosmic web like the real one; in 1998 two teams measuring distant exploding stars called Type Ia supernovae found them fainter than expected, showing the expansion is speeding up, and three scientists shared the Nobel Prize in 2011; Dark energy is the name for the unknown cause, and the simplest idea is that empty space has a constant energy of its own, Einstein's old cosmological constant; ordinary matter is about 5 per cent of the universe, dark matter about a quarter and dark energy about two thirds; the quantum estimate of the energy of empty space is far too big, off by an enormous factor, perhaps the worst prediction in physics; recent surveys hint that dark energy may be changing over time, but this is not settled; Zwicky, Rubin, Supernovae.
Chapter 17: nobody knows whether time began with the Big Bang or whether something came before it; speculative ideas include a Bounce from an earlier universe, a cycle of universes, and eternal inflation, and none has been tested; the observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across today, bigger than the age of the universe suggests because space stretched while the light travelled; measurements show that space is flat to within a small error, which does not say whether it is infinite; Entropy is a measure of disorder, and the second law says it tends to increase, which is why a cup of tea cools and a dropped egg does not unbreak; a shuffled deck of cards is far more likely to be messy than ordered; why the early universe had such low entropy is unsolved; there is no single universal now, and clocks of moving or high-up observers tick at different rates, so an astronaut on the International Space Station ages a few thousandths of a second less in six months; travel to the future by fast motion is real in principle, but no known way to travel to the past; the Multiverse is a speculative idea of many universes, not yet testable; Time travel, Paradox.
Chapter 18 (the far future, predictions not certainties, and the text says so): the Sun grows about ten per cent brighter every billion years and in perhaps a billion years the oceans will probably boil away; in about five billion years the Sun will swell into a Red giant and swallow Mercury and Venus and perhaps the Earth; it will then shed its outer layers as a glowing shell called a Planetary nebula and leave a White dwarf the size of the Earth that cools for trillions of years; the Milky Way and Andromeda are approaching and may merge in about five billion years, though a recent study says this is less certain than thought; stars are so far apart that few would collide; star formation will fade and the last stars will die after about a hundred trillion years; if dark energy goes on, galaxies beyond our own group will drift out of sight in a hundred billion years or more; Black dwarf, Brown dwarf; neutron stars and black holes will outlast stars, and black holes may slowly evaporate over times as long as a one followed by a hundred zeros years; the leading future is the Big Freeze or Heat death, a cold, dark, ever-expanding universe; a Big Crunch needs expansion to reverse and a Big Rip needs dark energy to grow, and neither is favoured by present evidence; Vacuum decay is a speculative possibility; Proton decay has never been seen; we live very early, less than one hundredth of one per cent of the way through the age of stars.
Chapter 19: a bigger mirror collects more light, so telescopes are light buckets; the Hubble Space Telescope (1990) sees above the blurring air and the James Webb Space Telescope sees infrared; radio, infrared, X-ray and gamma-ray telescopes show different things, and the FAST radio dish in China is 500 metres wide; Spectroscopy splits starlight into a rainbow with dark lines that reveal which elements are present, and helium was first found in the Sun's light in 1868 before anyone found it on Earth; Parallax, the shift of a star against the background as the Earth moves round the Sun, was first measured in 1838 and is the first step of the distance ladder, followed by Cepheids and supernovae; the Gaia satellite has mapped the positions of nearly two billion stars; the Super-Kamiokande detector in Japan lies deep underground and neutrino detectors caught neutrinos from a supernova in 1987; computer simulations build virtual universes; science works by guessing, testing and dropping ideas that fail, as when the glow of the Big Bang defeated the rival Steady state idea; the age of the universe measured by stars, the glow and the expansion agrees at nearly fourteen billion years; in 2011 an experiment seemed to show neutrinos faster than light and the cause was a loose cable, and the claim was withdrawn; amateur astronomers find comets and exploding stars; Telescope, Satellites.
Chapter 20: in 1990 Voyager 1 turned its camera back and photographed the Earth from about six billion kilometres away as a tiny dot of light, less than one pixel; people in every culture have told stories about where everything came from, and science adds a way of testing ideas; the same star atoms are in every person; Galileo's four moons of Jupiter can be seen with ordinary binoculars; new instruments such as the Vera Rubin Observatory, the Extremely Large Telescope and the LISA space detector of gravitational waves are being built or have just begun to work; Dawn, Binoculars, Pale blue dot.
chapters: The Spark That Is Still a Mystery
The Dark Part of the Universe

beats.scene: A person sits on a dark hilltop looking up at the stars
beats.summary: On a clear night on a hilltop, you look up and ask where everything came from.

beats.scene: Eyes slowly adjusting to the dark as more and more stars appear
beats.summary: As your eyes adjust to the dark, more and more stars appear, until the sky is crowded with them.

beats.scene: Lines join bright stars into the shapes of a hunter and a bear
beats.summary: People long ago joined the stars into pictures, but the stars in one picture are not really neighbours.

beats.scene: A steady bright planet moves among twinkling stars, night after night
beats.summary: A few bright lights do not twinkle and slowly change place from night to night: they are planets, the wanderers.

beats.scene: The full Moon hangs over the hilltop as a beam of light crosses
beats.summary: The Moon is the nearest world, about 384,000 kilometres away, and its light takes a little over a second to reach you.

beats.scene: A bright streak of light races around a small blue Earth several times
beats.summary: Light is the fastest thing there is, about 300,000 kilometres every second, enough to circle the Earth more than seven times in a second.

beats.scene: A golden beam crosses the dark gap between the Sun and the Earth
beats.summary: Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach the Earth, so you always see the Sun as it was eight minutes ago.

beats.scene: A long ruler of light stretches into space, marked with a single year
beats.summary: Astronomers measure the huge distances between stars in light-years, and one light-year is almost ten million million kilometres.

beats.scene: A small red star glows faintly as its light travels towards Earth
beats.summary: The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is a little over four light-years away, so its light left it more than four years ago.

beats.scene: A telescope on a hill points at a faint star, a clock behind
beats.summary: Because light takes time, looking at distant things means looking into the past, so a telescope is a kind of time machine.

beats.scene: A small yellow Sun beside a tiny Earth for comparison
beats.summary: The Sun is an ordinary star, but it is huge: about 1,300,000 Earths could fit inside it, and it holds nearly all the mass of the solar system.

beats.scene: Eight planets on round paths in a row around the Sun
beats.summary: Eight planets travel around the Sun, and the four closest to it, Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, are small and rocky.

beats.scene: A small grey scorched planet beside a bright cloudy planet
beats.summary: Mercury is small and scorched by the Sun; Venus is wrapped in thick clouds and is the hottest planet of all, about 465 degrees.

beats.scene: A red dusty planet with dry river beds and a small rover
beats.summary: Mars is cold, dry and red with dust, but it once had rivers and lakes, and robot rovers are exploring it today.

beats.scene: A wide ring of grey rocks of every size between Mars and Jupiter
beats.summary: Between Mars and Jupiter lies the asteroid belt, a ring of rocky leftovers from the making of the planets, with lots of empty space between them.

beats.scene: A giant striped planet with a huge red storm, a small Earth beside
beats.summary: Jupiter is the biggest planet, made mostly of gas, with a storm called the Great Red Spot that is larger than the Earth.

beats.scene: A planet with bright wide rings made of ice floating in the dark
beats.summary: Saturn is famous for its bright rings, made of billions of pieces of ice and rock, and it is so light for its size that it would float on water if there were a bath big enough.

beats.scene: Two pale blue planets far from a tiny Sun in the cold dark
beats.summary: Uranus and Neptune are cold blue worlds far from the Sun, and Neptune was found in 1846 by calculation before anyone saw it.

beats.scene: A dirty snowball with a long glowing tail points away from the Sun
beats.summary: Beyond Neptune lie small icy worlds like Pluto, and comets, dirty snowballs whose tails of gas stream away from the Sun, such as Halley's Comet every 76 years.

beats.scene: A tiny space probe flies away from the Sun into a dark empty gap
beats.summary: Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is the farthest human-made object, more than twenty billion kilometres away, yet it has barely left our own back garden of space.

beats.scene: Stars of blue, white and red glow in different colours across the dark
beats.summary: Stars have different colours: hot ones glow blue, middling ones like the Sun glow yellow-white, and cooler ones glow red.

beats.scene: A pale river of stars arching over a dark hill
beats.summary: The pale band across the sky is the Milky Way, our own galaxy seen from inside, and it holds at least a hundred billion stars.

beats.scene: A flat spiral of stars seen from above, the Sun far from the centre
beats.summary: From above, the Milky Way is a flat spiral about 100,000 light-years across, and the Sun sits in its outer suburbs, about 26,000 light-years from the centre.

beats.scene: The Sun moves on a huge circle around the glowing galactic centre
beats.summary: The Sun and its planets travel around the centre of the galaxy, taking about 230 million years for one full circle.

beats.scene: A pink glowing cloud of gas and dust with newborn stars shining inside it
beats.summary: In giant clouds of gas and dust, called nebulae, new stars are being born right now; the Orion Nebula, about 1,300 light-years away, can be seen with the eye as a faint fuzzy patch.

beats.scene: A huge red star beside a small yellow Sun and a dim dwarf
beats.summary: Stars come in very different sizes: red giants like Betelgeuse could swallow the inner planets, but most stars are small, dim red dwarfs.

beats.scene: A faint oval smudge of light in the sky above the hilltop
beats.summary: Andromeda looks like a faint smudge, but it is another great galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years away, and the farthest thing we can see with the eye alone.

beats.scene: Galaxies of different shapes, spirals, balls and ragged ones, float in the dark
beats.summary: Galaxies have many shapes, such as spirals, smooth balls called ellipticals and ragged irregulars, and the Milky Way and Andromeda belong to a small group of dozens of galaxies.

beats.scene: A telescope stares at a tiny dark patch that fills with thousands of galaxies
beats.summary: In 1995 the Hubble Space Telescope stared for about ten days at a tiny, empty-looking patch of sky and found about 3,000 galaxies.

beats.scene: Galaxies gather in glowing threads and clusters around huge dark empty bubbles
beats.summary: Galaxies are not scattered evenly: they gather in clusters and long threads, like a web, with huge empty voids between them.

beats.scene: Ancient farmers and sailors watch the Sun and stars rise over the sea
beats.summary: For thousands of years people watched the sky to know when to plant, when to sail and when the seasons would change.

beats.scene: The Earth's curved shadow crosses the face of the Moon
beats.summary: The ancient Greeks saw that the Earth is round: its shadow on the Moon during an eclipse is always curved, and ships sink below the horizon hull first.

beats.scene: A man in Alexandria measures a stick's shadow, while sunlight fills a distant well
beats.summary: Around 240 BC Eratosthenes compared the length of shadows in two cities and worked out how big the Earth is, close to the real figure of about 40,000 kilometres around.

beats.scene: An astronomer draws circles upon circles around a central Earth
beats.summary: About 150 AD Ptolemy described a system with the Earth at the centre, using circles on circles to predict where the planets would be, and it worked well enough for about 1,400 years.

beats.scene: A man on a ship looks at the still Earth and the moving sky
beats.summary: An Earth-centred sky felt natural: the ground does not seem to move, and the Sun, Moon and stars seem to travel across the sky, though one Greek, Aristarchus, had suggested that the Sun was at the centre.

beats.scene: A planet's path through the stars draws a backward loop
beats.summary: Sometimes a planet seems to stop and move backwards for a few weeks before going forwards again, a puzzle that the Earth-centred system could explain only with extra circles.

beats.scene: Copernicus holds a book showing the Sun in the middle, planets circling
beats.summary: In 1543 Copernicus published a book putting the Sun at the centre, with the Earth spinning once a day and going around the Sun once a year, which explained the backward loops simply.

beats.scene: A man writes long columns of numbers beside a sky chart with oval paths
beats.summary: Tycho Brahe measured the planets' positions very carefully by eye, and in 1609 Johannes Kepler used these numbers to show that planets move on ovals, not circles.

beats.scene: Galileo points a small telescope at Jupiter and its four tiny moons
beats.summary: In 1610 Galileo pointed a telescope at Jupiter and saw four small moons going around it, proof that not everything circles the Earth.

beats.scene: An old man in a plain room is watched by judges in dark robes
beats.summary: Galileo also saw Venus show phases like the Moon, which fits the Sun-centred system; in 1633 the Church made him take back his claim, and he lived the rest of his life under house arrest.

beats.scene: An apple falls from a tree while the Moon hangs in the evening sky
beats.summary: In the 1600s Isaac Newton asked why an apple falls to the ground but the Moon does not, and realised that it might be the same pull acting on both.

beats.scene: A cannonball fired from a mountain top curves around the whole Earth
beats.summary: Newton imagined a cannonball fired from a mountain: fire it fast enough and it falls all the way around the Earth, which is just what the Moon is doing.

beats.scene: A great book opens to show two balls pulling on each other
beats.summary: In 1687 Newton published his law of gravity: every object pulls on every other object, heavier things pull harder, and the pull gets weaker with distance.

beats.scene: A comet returns to the sky above a crowd looking up at night
beats.summary: Edmond Halley used Newton's law to predict that a bright comet would return in 1758, and when it did, years after Halley had died, the law was proved right.

beats.scene: A small planet circles a bright Sun on a path that slowly turns
beats.summary: There was one small puzzle: the orbit of Mercury turns a tiny bit more than Newton's law says it should, and for decades nobody knew why.

beats.scene: A young man at a desk beside a clock and a beam of light
beats.summary: In 1905 Albert Einstein showed that light has the same speed for everyone, however they move, and that this makes time run differently for people moving in different ways.

beats.scene: A heavy ball sinks into a stretched blanket while a marble rolls around it
beats.summary: In 1915 Einstein's general relativity said that mass bends space and time, and objects move along the curves, so gravity is not a pull but the shape of space and time.

beats.scene: Stars shine slightly out of place beside the Sun in an eclipse
beats.summary: In 1919, during an eclipse, Arthur Eddington's expeditions saw that the light of stars bent as it passed the Sun, just as Einstein had predicted, and Einstein became famous.

beats.scene: A galaxy bends the light of a faraway galaxy into a bright ring
beats.summary: Heavy galaxies bend light like a giant lens, and with telescopes we now see far-off galaxies stretched into arcs and rings by the gravity of those in front.

beats.scene: A satellite orbits the Earth, its clock ticking faster than one on the ground
beats.summary: Time runs slightly faster high above the Earth than on the ground, and navigation satellites have to correct for this or their errors would grow by kilometres in a day.

beats.scene: A great star sinks inward as gravity wins over the fading heat inside
beats.summary: A star is a balance between gravity pulling in and heat pushing out, and when a very heavy star runs out of fuel, gravity wins and the core falls inward.

beats.scene: A rocket rises from the ground and a stronger pull holds a heavier world
beats.summary: To escape the Earth you need to go about eleven kilometres a second; on a much heavier world you would need to go faster, and one day that speed would be faster than light.

beats.scene: A tiny dark ball replaces the Sun in a black sky
beats.summary: A black hole forms when a huge amount of matter is squeezed into a tiny space; if the Sun became one, it would be only about six kilometres across.

beats.scene: A spaceship nears a dark circle that bends the stars behind it
beats.summary: The edge of a black hole is called the event horizon, a point of no return rather than a solid surface; anything that crosses it, even light, can never come back out.

beats.scene: Hot bright gas spirals around a dark centre and glows with X-rays
beats.summary: We cannot see a black hole, but we find them by the hot gas that spirals into them and glows with X-rays, as in Cygnus X-1, or by the way nearby stars move.

beats.scene: A small planet circles quietly around a black hole
beats.summary: Black holes are not cosmic vacuum cleaners: if the Sun turned into one, the Earth would keep circling it just as before, only in the dark.

beats.scene: A bright centre of a galaxy with stars racing around an invisible point
beats.summary: At the centre of the Milky Way sits a black hole about four million times heavier than the Sun, shown by years of following stars that race around nothing we can see.

beats.scene: A ring of glowing gas around a dark centre
beats.summary: In 2019 a network of radio dishes across the Earth made the first picture of a black hole's shadow, in the galaxy Messier 87, about 55 million light-years away.

beats.scene: A clock beside a black hole ticks slowly and fades
beats.summary: Near a black hole time slows down: to someone far away, a clock falling in seems to tick more and more slowly and fade out, though to the falling clock all is normal.

beats.scene: A tiny bright point at the heart of a dark circle
beats.summary: Nobody knows what happens at the very centre of a black hole, because our theories break down there; theory also suggests that black holes slowly lose energy and could shrink over unimaginably long times.

beats.scene: An astronomer at a telescope wonders if the Milky Way is all there is
beats.summary: Until the 1920s many astronomers thought the Milky Way was the whole universe, and that the fuzzy spirals seen in telescopes were small clouds inside it.

beats.scene: A woman at a desk studies rows of glass plates of pulsing stars
beats.summary: Around 1912 Henrietta Leavitt found that certain pulsing stars flash more slowly the brighter they really are, which gave astronomers a yardstick for measuring distance.

beats.scene: A man at a huge mountain telescope observes the Andromeda smudge
beats.summary: In 1924 Edwin Hubble found a pulsing star in Andromeda, measured its distance, and showed that Andromeda lies far outside the Milky Way: it is a galaxy of its own.

beats.scene: A siren-shaped sound wave stretches while a light wave turns from blue to red
beats.summary: When a siren speeds away from you its sound drops in pitch, and when a galaxy speeds away its light shifts towards red, called redshift.

beats.scene: A graph of dots climbing in a line above far galaxies
beats.summary: In 1929 Hubble showed that the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away from us, an idea that Georges Lemaître had also worked out from theory in 1927.

beats.scene: Raisins in rising dough drift apart as the dough swells in an oven
beats.summary: The galaxies are not flying through space: space itself is stretching, like dough with raisins in it, and every raisin moves away from every other.

beats.scene: A balloon with dots on its skin swells, the dots moving apart
beats.summary: The expansion has no centre: from any galaxy, all the others seem to be moving away, just as every dot on an inflating balloon moves away from every other dot.

beats.scene: Einstein looks at a page of equations beside a crossed-out symbol
beats.summary: Einstein had added an extra term to his equations to keep the universe still, and when expansion was found he dropped it; the story goes that he called it his greatest blunder.

beats.scene: A galaxy cluster holds together while empty space widens between distant clusters
beats.summary: Things held together by gravity and other forces do not expand: your body, the Earth and the Milky Way stay the same size, and only the great gaps between galaxy groups grow.

beats.scene: A ruler of light marks galaxy distances beside two measuring tapes that disagree slightly
beats.summary: Astronomers now find that each million light-years of distance adds about twenty kilometres a second to a galaxy's speed, though two ways of measuring it give slightly different answers, an open puzzle.

beats.scene: A film strip runs backward as galaxies crowd together into a glowing point
beats.summary: If the universe is expanding, then long ago everything was closer together and hotter; nearly fourteen billion years ago it was extremely hot and dense.

beats.scene: A grid of lines stretches evenly in every direction as dots spread apart
beats.summary: The Big Bang was not an explosion in one place: space itself began to expand everywhere at once, so there is no centre and no outside to it.

beats.scene: A man speaks into an old radio microphone beside a blackboard
beats.summary: The name Big Bang was coined by the astronomer Fred Hoyle in a radio talk in 1949; he favoured a rival idea, but the name stuck.

beats.scene: A glowing speck floats in darkness beside a blank blackboard
beats.summary: Physics can follow the universe back to a tiny fraction of a second after the beginning, but the very first moment is unknown, because our theories cannot describe it.

beats.scene: A tiny bright speck swells hugely in a sudden flash of light
beats.summary: Inflation is the idea that in a tiny fraction of a second the universe grew enormously, which would explain why it is so smooth; it is a leading idea, not yet proved.

beats.scene: A hot bright soup of tiny particles swirls and cools into larger ones
beats.summary: At first it was too hot even for the cores of atoms; the universe was a soup of particles called quarks, which at about a millionth of a second began to join into protons and neutrons.

beats.scene: Bright flashes where pairs of matching particles meet and vanish, leaving a few behind
beats.summary: Every particle has an opposite called antimatter, and when the two meet they destroy each other; a tiny surplus of matter, about one part in a billion, survived, and nobody knows why.

beats.scene: Protons and neutrons join into helium cores in a glowing, hot cloud
beats.summary: Within the first few minutes, when the universe was still hotter than the middle of a star, protons and neutrons joined to make the cores of helium and a little lithium.

beats.scene: Old gas glows in a telescope beside a chart of three parts to one
beats.summary: The result was about three quarters hydrogen and one quarter helium by mass, a mix that calculations in the 1940s predicted and that the oldest gas clouds still show today.

beats.scene: A dim glowing fog fills all of space
beats.summary: For about 380,000 years the universe stayed a hot, glowing fog in which light could not travel far, because free particles kept scattering it.

beats.scene: Particles join into the first atoms as a bright fog clears across space
beats.summary: At about 380,000 years the universe had cooled to about 3,000 degrees, electrons joined with nuclei to form the first atoms, and light was suddenly free to travel.

beats.scene: A faint orange glow spreads evenly across the whole sky in every direction
beats.summary: That ancient light has been travelling ever since, stretched by the expansion from bright light into weak microwaves, and it now fills the whole sky at about 270 degrees below zero.

beats.scene: Two men beside a large horn-shaped antenna on a hill listen to a hiss
beats.summary: In 1964 and 1965 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson found an unexplained hiss in their antenna that came from every direction, even after they cleaned out the pigeons' droppings, and it proved to be that ancient light.

beats.scene: An old television set with a snowy screen of static in a dark room
beats.summary: A small part of the static on an old television set between channels came from the Big Bang; so you may once have seen the oldest light in the universe without knowing it.

beats.scene: A satellite in space draws a speckled colour map of the whole sky
beats.summary: Satellites named COBE, WMAP and Planck mapped the glow and found that it is almost perfectly even, with tiny ripples of about one part in 100,000.

beats.scene: Denser patches in a gas cloud pull in more gas
beats.summary: The tiny ripples were seeds: places that were slightly denser pulled in more matter by gravity, and over hundreds of millions of years they grew into galaxies and clusters of galaxies.

beats.scene: Utter darkness, a faint red glow at one edge and clouds of gas
beats.summary: After the glow faded, the universe was dark for hundreds of millions of years, with no stars yet, only clouds of hydrogen and helium; astronomers call this time the dark ages.

beats.scene: The first stars blaze blue-white like lamps in a fog
beats.summary: A few hundred million years after the beginning, the first stars switched on: huge, hot, blue and short-lived, though we have not yet seen one directly.

beats.scene: Bright light from young stars splits clouds of gas around them into clear bubbles
beats.summary: The fierce light of these early stars broke the hydrogen gas around them apart, clearing the cosmic fog a second time in an era called reionisation.

beats.scene: A great gold-mirrored telescope in space looks at tiny red smudges of faraway galaxies
beats.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, sees infrared light and has found galaxies from less than 400 million years after the beginning, some surprisingly bright and large.

beats.scene: A dark cloud of gas collapses into a swirling ball that begins to glow
beats.summary: A star begins when a cloud of gas collapses under its own gravity; as the ball shrinks it squeezes and heats, and starts to glow.

beats.scene: The heart of a young star flashes into brilliant light as fusion starts
beats.summary: When the core reaches about ten million degrees, hydrogen cores begin to fuse together, and the star ignites.

beats.scene: Four small balls merge into one, with a tiny flash of light
beats.summary: In the Sun, four hydrogen cores fuse into one helium core, and a tiny amount of mass turns into energy; every second the Sun turns about four million tonnes of mass into light and heat.

beats.scene: A glowing star with arrows pushing out and pulling in
beats.summary: A star stays steady because the heat from fusion pushes outwards just as hard as gravity pulls inwards; the Sun's core is about 15 million degrees, and light takes many thousands of years to work its way out.

beats.scene: A giant blue star burns brightly beside a tiny red star that glows quietly
beats.summary: Heavy stars burn fast and die in a few million years, while the smallest red dwarfs burn so slowly that they may shine for trillions of years; the Sun is about halfway through a life of ten billion years.

beats.scene: A giant star with layers like an onion, with iron at the very centre
beats.summary: When a heavy star uses up its hydrogen, it fuses helium into carbon and oxygen, and the biggest stars go on, layer by layer, up to iron, which gives no energy when it fuses.

beats.scene: A star bursts open in a huge bright flash that fills a distant galaxy
beats.summary: When the iron core collapses, the star explodes as a supernova, which for a few weeks can shine as brightly as a whole galaxy; Chinese astronomers recorded one in 1054, and its remains are the Crab Nebula.

beats.scene: A tiny dense ball spins and sends out beams of light
beats.summary: What is left of the core can be a neutron star, a ball as small as a city but as heavy as the Sun, so dense that a teaspoon of it would weigh about two billion tonnes; spinning ones that flash are called pulsars.

beats.scene: Two tiny dense stars collide in a flash of light
beats.summary: Many of the heaviest elements, such as gold and platinum, are made when two neutron stars collide; in 2017 astronomers saw such a collision in both gravitational waves and light.

beats.scene: A dying star scatters glowing clouds that gather into new stars
beats.summary: Dying stars scatter their atoms into space, and these enrich the gas from which new stars and planets form, so the Sun is probably a later generation of star, built from the ashes of older ones.

beats.scene: A child holds out a hand beneath a glowing night sky
beats.summary: Nearly all the atoms in your body were made long ago: the hydrogen in the Big Bang, and almost everything else, such as the carbon, oxygen and iron, inside stars.

beats.scene: A cloud of gas and dust begins to fall inwards towards its own centre
beats.summary: About 4,600 million years ago a cloud of gas and dust, perhaps nudged by a nearby exploding star, began to collapse, and that cloud became the Sun and everything that circles it.

beats.scene: A young bright star in the middle of a flat spinning disc of dust
beats.summary: As the cloud collapsed it spun faster and flattened into a disc; the Sun formed in the middle, and the leftover gas and dust circled around it.

beats.scene: Dust grains stick into pebbles, then rocks, then small worlds in a wide disc
beats.summary: In the disc, dust stuck into pebbles, pebbles into rocks and rocks into small worlds, which over tens of millions of years grew into planets: rocky ones near the Sun and huge gas ones beyond.

beats.scene: A glowing red-hot ball of rock with rivers of liquid fire on it
beats.summary: The young Earth was hot enough to be partly melted; heavy iron sank to the centre and formed the core, while lighter rock floated above it.

beats.scene: A huge rock hits the young Earth in a blaze of fire
beats.summary: Most scientists think the Moon formed when a body about the size of Mars, called Theia, hit the young Earth; the debris gathered into a ball and became the Moon.

beats.scene: Rain pours down on a rocky young Earth and fills shallow seas with water
beats.summary: As the Earth cooled, water gathered into oceans; where it came from is still debated, partly from the Earth's own rocks and perhaps partly from asteroids and comets.

beats.scene: The Moon rises over an ocean and the tide rolls in on a shore
beats.summary: The Moon pulls on the oceans to make the tides and helps keep the Earth's tilt steady, and it is slowly drifting away from us by about four centimetres a year.

beats.scene: Glowing curved lines protect a blue planet from a stream of particles
beats.summary: The Earth's iron core makes a magnetic field, which acts like a shield and keeps the stream of particles from the Sun from stripping away the air.

beats.scene: A small blue world sits at the right distance from a warm Sun
beats.summary: The Earth lies in the habitable zone, not too hot and not too cold, where water can stay liquid on the surface; so after about four and a half billion years of building, the stage was ready.

beats.scene: Layered mounds of rock grow in a warm shallow sea under a young sky
beats.summary: Life appeared on Earth early: the oldest signs, such as layered rock mounds made by tiny microbes, are more than 3,500 million years old.

beats.scene: Sparks flash inside a glass flask of simple gases and water
beats.summary: In 1952 Stanley Miller and Harold Urey sent sparks through a flask of simple gases and water, and found they had made amino acids, the building blocks of proteins.

beats.scene: A rocky meteorite splits open in a field to show tiny grains inside
beats.summary: In 1969 the Murchison meteorite fell in Australia, and it held many amino acids, which shows that some of the ingredients of life are made in space.

beats.scene: Hot springs on a dark sea floor send up clouds of warm mineral water
beats.summary: Where life began is debated: ideas include warm shallow pools, clay, and hot springs on the sea floor, called hydrothermal vents, which scientists found in 1977 teeming with life.

beats.scene: A strand of chemical code copies itself inside a tiny bubble of fat
beats.summary: One idea, the RNA world, says that a chemical called RNA, which can both store information and speed up reactions, may have come before cells, though this is not proved.

beats.scene: Green cells in sunlight release a stream of fine bubbles into the water
beats.summary: For about two billion years life stayed tiny and single-celled; then some cells learned to use sunlight and released oxygen, and about 2,400 million years ago they began to change the air.

beats.scene: A large cell swallows a smaller one beside a soft-bodied animal
beats.summary: Around two billion years ago, larger cells with a nucleus appeared, perhaps when one cell swallowed another, and animals followed about 600 million years ago.

beats.scene: A branching tree of living things with all branches joined at one root
beats.summary: Charles Darwin explained in 1859 how living things change over time by natural selection, and all life today shares the same DNA code, which points to a common ancestor.

beats.scene: A huge rock streaks towards the Earth above a herd of giant lizards
beats.summary: Life has often been shaken by disasters: about 66 million years ago an asteroid struck the Earth and ended the dinosaurs, which gave small furry animals, the mammals, their chance.

beats.scene: A small clock face with a tiny final slice of time marked for humans
beats.summary: If the history of the Earth were one day long, our own species would appear only in the last six seconds, and all of written history would fit into a blink.

beats.scene: Two astronomers beside a dome at night looking at a wobbling star
beats.summary: Until 1995 nobody had found a planet around an ordinary star like the Sun; that year Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found one, and won a Nobel Prize for it.

beats.scene: A telescope watches a star dim as a small planet crosses
beats.summary: The Kepler space telescope, launched in 2009, found thousands of planets by watching for the tiny dimming of a star when a planet passes in front of it.

beats.scene: A sky map covered with thousands of tiny dots
beats.summary: More than 5,000 planets of other stars, called exoplanets, are now confirmed, and astronomers think that most stars have planets, so the Milky Way holds billions.

beats.scene: Strange planets: one close to its star, one with two suns
beats.summary: Many exoplanets are nothing like ours: giant planets that orbit closer to their stars than Mercury does, worlds with two suns, and many planets between the size of the Earth and Neptune, which our solar system lacks.

beats.scene: Seven rocky planets in a tight row around a small, dim red star
beats.summary: Some planets lie in the habitable zone of their star, such as Proxima b, found in 2016, and some of the seven rocky planets of the small star TRAPPIST-1, about 40 light-years away, but nobody knows whether any can support life.

beats.scene: Starlight passes through the thin glowing air of a planet
beats.summary: Telescopes such as the James Webb can study the air of another planet by the starlight that passes through it, looking for gases that might hint at life, though no such sign has been confirmed.

beats.scene: Ice cracks and water jets spray into space above a small moon
beats.summary: Closer to home, Mars once had water, Jupiter's moon Europa and Saturn's moon Enceladus have oceans of water under their ice, and a probe flew through Enceladus's geysers, but nothing alive has been found beyond Earth.

beats.scene: A giant radio dish listens at night beneath a sky full of stars
beats.summary: Since 1960 the search for radio signals from other civilisations, called SETI, has listened to the sky; the best-known mystery is the Wow signal of 1977, a strong burst lasting 72 seconds that was never heard again.

beats.scene: A lone figure on a hill looks at the sky
beats.summary: The Fermi question asks: if the galaxy is so old and so full of planets, why have we not met anyone? There are many suggested answers, but none is certain.

beats.scene: A small golden disc rides on a probe among the stars
beats.summary: In 1977 the two Voyager probes were sent off carrying golden records with greetings in 55 languages, music and the sounds of the Earth, like a message in a bottle; whether we are alone is still unknown.

beats.scene: A small magnet lifts a paper clip against the pull of the whole Earth
beats.summary: All the pushes and pulls in nature come from four forces; gravity is the weakest, as a small magnet shows when it lifts a paper clip against the pull of the whole Earth.

beats.scene: Lightning, a radio mast, a rainbow and a magnet shown together as one family
beats.summary: Electromagnetism is the force of electricity and magnetism and light; it holds atoms together and drives all of chemistry, and radio waves, microwaves, visible light and X-rays are all the same kind of wave.

beats.scene: Tiny particles are held together at the heart of an atom
beats.summary: The strong force holds the cores of atoms together against their own push, and the weak force causes some kinds of radioactivity and makes the fusion in the Sun possible.

beats.scene: A tiny marble in the middle of a huge empty stadium
beats.summary: An atom is almost all empty space: its core is about 100,000 times smaller than the whole atom, like a marble in the middle of a stadium, with electrons far away in the seats.

beats.scene: Three little balls inside a larger ball, ghostly particles passing through a hand
beats.summary: Protons and neutrons are each made of three smaller particles called quarks, and there are also ghostly particles called neutrinos, tens of billions of which from the Sun pass through your thumbnail every second.

beats.scene: A hot glowing object gives out light in tiny separate packets
beats.summary: In 1900 Max Planck found that energy comes in small packets called quanta, and in 1905 Einstein showed that light itself comes in packets, which we now call photons.

beats.scene: Electrons pass through two narrow slits and build a pattern of stripes
beats.summary: When electrons are sent one at a time through two narrow slits, they slowly build up a pattern of stripes, as waves would, as if each one had gone through both slits at once.

beats.scene: A pair of dice floats above a screen with a pattern of glowing chances
beats.summary: Quantum theory cannot say where one electron will land, only the chances of each place; this deeply troubled Einstein, though experiments keep supporting the theory.

beats.scene: A blurred ball inside a tiny box with a ruler and a stopwatch nearby
beats.summary: In 1927 Werner Heisenberg stated the uncertainty principle: we cannot know exactly both where a particle is and how it moves; this is part of nature and not a failure of our instruments.

beats.scene: A glowing laser beam, a computer chip and a medical scanner in a row
beats.summary: Quantum physics works superbly: it gave us lasers, transistors, computers, LEDs and body scanners, and it is among the most precisely tested theories ever, though scientists still argue about what it really means.

beats.scene: A chart of tiny particles arranged in neat rows
beats.summary: The Standard Model is the list of all the known particles and three of the four forces, and it matches experiments with astonishing precision.

beats.scene: A huge ring-shaped tunnel under the ground with two beams meeting in a flash
beats.summary: In 2012 the Higgs boson was found at CERN's Large Hadron Collider, a ring 27 kilometres round; the Higgs field is how particles get their mass.

beats.scene: A particle chart with large blank spaces left in it
beats.summary: The Standard Model is not the whole story: it leaves out gravity, dark matter and dark energy, and it cannot say why matter beat antimatter.

beats.scene: A big book of stars and a small book of atoms, side by side
beats.summary: General relativity describes the very big and quantum physics describes the very small, and each works superbly in its own world.

beats.scene: A black hole centre and a speck of the early universe
beats.summary: The two theories clash where something is both very heavy and very small, as at the centre of a black hole and at the very start of the universe, where gravity and quantum effects both matter.

beats.scene: An old man fills a blackboard with equations
beats.summary: Many physicists want a theory of everything that joins all the forces; Einstein spent his last decades looking for one and did not find it.

beats.scene: A tiny loop of string vibrates like a guitar string
beats.summary: String theory says that particles are tiny strings that vibrate in different ways, like notes on a guitar, and it needs extra hidden dimensions of space; it is mathematically beautiful but has never been tested.

beats.scene: A fine net of tiny grains makes up the fabric of space itself
beats.summary: A rival idea, loop quantum gravity, says that space itself is made of tiny grains; it is also untested, and there are other ideas as well.

beats.scene: A glowing machine as huge as a galaxy beside a tiny ordinary laboratory
beats.summary: Testing these ideas is very hard: the energies needed are far beyond any machine we can build, so physicists look to black holes and the early universe for hints.

beats.scene: Two black holes spiral together and send ripples across space
beats.summary: In 2015 the detector LIGO caught ripples in space-time, gravitational waves, from two black holes that merged about 1.3 billion light-years away, moving its arms by much less than the width of a proton.

beats.scene: Galaxies in a huge cluster swirl too fast around their common centre
beats.summary: In the 1930s Fritz Zwicky noticed that the galaxies in a cluster move far too fast to be held together by the matter we can see.

beats.scene: A spinning galaxy with a faint glowing halo of invisible matter drawn around it
beats.summary: In the 1970s Vera Rubin found that stars far out in galaxies orbit as fast as those near the middle, so each galaxy must hold a great deal of unseen mass.

beats.scene: A dark shape fills the space around a bright galaxy
beats.summary: This invisible stuff is called dark matter: it gives out no light and is felt only through its gravity, and there seems to be about five times as much of it as ordinary matter.

beats.scene: Two huge clusters collide, hot gas left behind, mass moving on
beats.summary: More evidence comes from lensing and from the Bullet Cluster, two galaxy clusters that collided: the gas was slowed down, but most of the mass passed straight through, as dark matter should.

beats.scene: A deep underground laboratory with a silent detector waiting in the dark
beats.summary: Nobody knows what dark matter is made of; detectors deep underground have not yet caught a single particle of it, and a few scientists try to change the law of gravity instead.

beats.scene: A web of glowing threads grows out of a dark cloud
beats.summary: Computer simulations that include dark matter grow a cosmic web just like the real one, so dark matter seems to have been the invisible scaffolding on which the galaxies were built.

beats.scene: A faraway star explosion looks dimmer than expected
beats.summary: In 1998 two teams measuring distant exploding stars found them fainter than expected, which showed that the expansion of the universe is not slowing down but speeding up.

beats.scene: An invisible pressure pushes outwards on a stretching grid of space
beats.summary: The unknown cause of the speeding-up is called dark energy; the simplest idea is that empty space itself has a constant energy, which is Einstein's old extra term, the cosmological constant, returning.

beats.scene: A circle divided into three parts, with one tiny slice glowing brightly
beats.summary: Ordinary matter is only about five per cent of the universe; dark matter is about a quarter and dark energy about two thirds, so we understand only a small slice of the whole.

beats.scene: A calculator shows an absurdly huge number next to a tiny measured one
beats.summary: When physicists use quantum theory to work out the energy of empty space, the answer is far too big, off by an enormous factor, perhaps the worst prediction in physics; recent surveys hint that dark energy may be changing, but this is not settled.

beats.scene: A great clock face fades into mist before its very first hour
beats.summary: Did time begin with the Big Bang? Nobody knows whether something came before it, or whether the question even makes sense.

beats.scene: A universe shrinks to a point and swells again like a bouncing ball
beats.summary: Some speculative ideas say our universe bounced out of an earlier one, or that universes go through cycles, or that new universes keep forming; none of these ideas has been tested.

beats.scene: A glowing sphere of galaxies surrounds a tiny observer in the middle
beats.summary: The observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across today; it is bigger than the age of the universe suggests because space stretched while the light was travelling.

beats.scene: Galaxies continue beyond the circle of what can be seen
beats.summary: What lies beyond the observable part is unknown; space seems to be flat, which fits with an endless universe, but it does not prove it.

beats.scene: A steaming cup of tea cools on a table beside a spoon
beats.summary: Time seems to run one way: a cup of tea cools down but never heats itself up, and a dropped egg never unbreaks.

beats.scene: A neat deck of cards beside the same cards in a messy heap
beats.summary: The answer is disorder, which physicists call entropy: there are far more messy arrangements than tidy ones, so things tend to become more disordered, just as a shuffled deck is almost never in order.

beats.scene: A tidy glowing early universe at the top of a long slope
beats.summary: Yet this raises a puzzle: for entropy to rise, the early universe must have started in an extremely orderly state, and why it did is unsolved.

beats.scene: An astronaut floats in a space station beside a clock
beats.summary: Time is not the same for everybody: moving fast or being high up changes how a clock ticks, so there is no single universal now; an astronaut in the space station ages a few thousandths of a second less in six months.

beats.scene: A traveller steps out of a fast rocket into a changed world
beats.summary: In principle a fast traveller could travel into the future, because a journey at nearly the speed of light would pass slowly for the traveller; but nobody knows any way to travel into the past.

beats.scene: Many bubble universes float in a dark sea
beats.summary: Some physicists wonder whether our universe is only one of many, a multiverse; it is a speculative idea that nobody has been able to test so far.

beats.scene: A dry hot Earth lies under a large bright Sun in a pale sky
beats.summary: The Sun is slowly getting brighter, about ten per cent every billion years, and in perhaps a billion years the Earth will probably be too hot for oceans.

beats.scene: A swollen red Sun fills the sky above a scorched grey rocky world
beats.summary: In about five billion years the Sun will use up the hydrogen in its core and swell into a red giant, swallowing Mercury and Venus and perhaps the Earth.

beats.scene: A glowing shell of gas surrounds a tiny white star in the dark
beats.summary: After that the Sun will shed its outer layers as a glowing shell and leave behind a white dwarf, a hot ember about the size of the Earth that slowly cools over trillions of years.

beats.scene: Two great spiral galaxies approach each other with their arms stretching into long tails
beats.summary: The Milky Way and Andromeda are drawing closer, and they may merge in about five billion years, although a recent study says this is less certain; since stars are far apart, few will collide.

beats.scene: Old red stars dim one by one in a darkening sky
beats.summary: New stars form more and more slowly, because the gas is running out, and after about a hundred trillion years or so the last stars will go out.

beats.scene: One small galaxy glows while distant galaxies fade away
beats.summary: If dark energy continues as it is, galaxies beyond our own group will drift out of sight in a hundred billion years or more, leaving future astronomers with a lonely sky.

beats.scene: A cold dark sky holds only drifting dead stars and a few black holes
beats.summary: Dead stars such as white dwarfs and neutron stars will grow cold, while black holes will last the longest, and theory says that even they may slowly evaporate over times like a one followed by a hundred zeros years.

beats.scene: A vast cold universe stretches out in darkness
beats.summary: The leading idea for the end is the Big Freeze, or heat death: the universe keeps expanding, cooling and thinning until it is cold, dark and nearly empty.

beats.scene: Three paths split from a glowing point, each to a different sky
beats.summary: Other endings have been suggested: a Big Crunch needs the expansion to reverse, a Big Rip needs dark energy to grow, and a bubble of different space might in theory appear; present evidence does not favour them.

beats.scene: A small bright candle burns at the start of a long road
beats.summary: We live very early: the age of stars will last about a hundred trillion years, and we are less than one hundredth of one per cent of the way through it.

beats.scene: A great telescope mirror in a dome gathers a faint spot of light
beats.summary: A telescope is a light bucket: the bigger its mirror, the more faint light it collects; the Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, sees clearly above the blurring air.

beats.scene: Telescopes of different shapes see one galaxy in different colours
beats.summary: Telescopes also collect radio waves, infrared, X-rays and gamma rays, and each kind of light shows something different; the FAST radio dish in China is 500 metres wide.

beats.scene: Starlight passes through a prism and spreads into a rainbow with dark lines
beats.summary: Splitting starlight into a rainbow, called a spectrum, shows dark lines that reveal which elements a star contains; helium was found in the Sun's light in 1868, before anyone found it on Earth.

beats.scene: A ladder of steps from near stars to far galaxies
beats.summary: To measure distances, astronomers use a ladder of methods: first the shift of a star against the background as the Earth moves, then pulsing stars, then exploding stars, each step checking the next.

beats.scene: A satellite scans the sky and plots a huge star map
beats.summary: The Gaia satellite has mapped the positions and motions of nearly two billion stars, giving us a three-dimensional map of a large part of our galaxy.

beats.scene: A huge tank of water deep underground is lined with golden light sensors
beats.summary: Deep underground, huge detectors watch for neutrinos from the Sun and from exploding stars; in 1987 they caught a burst from a supernova that was seen a few hours later in the sky.

beats.scene: A glowing screen shows a virtual universe growing
beats.summary: Supercomputers grow virtual universes from the start, following gravity and gas, and then compare them with real surveys, which lets scientists test ideas that no laboratory could.

beats.scene: Two rival ideas on a scale, tipped by a faint glow
beats.summary: Science works by guessing, testing and dropping ideas that fail: the glow of the Big Bang defeated its rival, the Steady State idea, which could not explain it.

beats.scene: A scientist finds a loose cable behind a screen of numbers
beats.summary: Science corrects itself: in 2011 an experiment seemed to show neutrinos travelling faster than light, but the cause was a loose cable, and the claim was withdrawn.

beats.scene: A person with a small backyard telescope sees a bright comet at dawn
beats.summary: Anyone can take part: amateur astronomers with ordinary telescopes find comets and exploding stars, and many of today's discoveries come from the shared work of thousands of people.

beats.scene: A winding road of glowing scenes from first spark to blue world
beats.summary: The whole story in one breath: space began to expand, hydrogen and helium formed, the first stars lit up and made the elements, planets and then life appeared, and now we ask about it.

beats.scene: A stone bridge on one bank, a misty gap on the other
beats.summary: Some parts are firmly known: the expansion, the glow of the Big Bang, the mix of the first elements, the way stars work; other parts remain open, such as what came before, dark matter, dark energy and how life began.

beats.scene: A pale blue speck of dust floats in a long beam of sunlight
beats.summary: In 1990 Voyager 1 turned its camera back and photographed the Earth from about six billion kilometres away: a tiny dot of light, less than one pixel, in a beam of sunlight.

beats.scene: A small figure sits beneath a vast sky holding a glowing lantern
beats.summary: We are tiny in a vast universe, yet we are the part of it that can wonder and understand: through us, the universe looks at itself.

beats.scene: People around fires tell stories about the sky
beats.summary: People in every culture have told stories about where everything came from, and science adds one more thing: a way of testing ideas against the evidence, and changing them when they fail.

beats.scene: People of many colours and ages stand together under one sky and point upwards
beats.summary: The same star atoms are in every one of us, and all people on Earth share the same sky and the same small planet.

beats.scene: A person looks at Jupiter and four moons through binoculars
beats.summary: You can see for yourself: with ordinary binoculars, on a clear night, you can see the four moons of Jupiter that Galileo found, and a dark sky can show you the Milky Way and Andromeda.

beats.scene: A new giant telescope and a space detector prepare to look at the sky
beats.summary: The next answers may come soon: new instruments, such as the Vera Rubin Observatory, the Extremely Large Telescope and the LISA detector, have begun or are being built, and each will look at the sky in a new way.

beats.scene: Dawn spreads above the hill as the stars begin to fade
beats.summary: As dawn comes, the stars fade and the Sun rises, its light eight minutes old; you start to leave the hilltop, but your view of the sky has changed.

beats.scene: The same hilltop at night, with the traveller smiling up at the stars
beats.summary: Back on the hilltop, the sky is the same, but now you can read some of its story, and many questions remain open; the next chapter may be written by someone who is just now looking up.

A new space telescope can see very early galaxies.
