B1B2: Imagine you are sitting on a hilltop on a clear, dark night. Above you, thousands of stars are shining, and you start to wonder where it all came from.
After about twenty minutes, your eyes have grown used to the dark. Stars that were invisible at first begin to appear, and soon the sky is crowded with them.
People long ago joined bright stars into pictures, such as a hunter, a bear and a swan. These patterns are called constellations, but the stars in one pattern are not really neighbours.
A few of the bright lights do not twinkle, and they slowly change their place from one night to the next. The ancient Greeks called them wanderers, and today we call them planets.
The Moon is our nearest neighbour in space, about 384,000 kilometres away. Its light takes a little more than one second to reach your eyes.
Nothing in the universe travels faster than light, which covers about 300,000 kilometres in every second. In that single second it could race around the whole Earth more than seven times.
The Sun is much farther away than the Moon, and its light takes about eight minutes to reach the Earth. So whenever you look at the Sun, you see it as it was eight minutes ago.
Distances between the stars are so huge that astronomers measure them in light-years. One light-year is the distance light travels in a year, which is almost ten million million kilometres.
The nearest star after the Sun is a faint red star called Proxima Centauri. It is a little more than four light-years away, so the light you see tonight left it over four years ago.
Because light takes time to travel, looking far away also means looking into the past. In this way, a telescope is a kind of time machine, and the farther it looks, the older the light it collects.
The Sun is an ordinary star, yet it is enormous. About 1,300,000 Earths could fit inside it, and it holds nearly all the mass of our solar system.
Eight planets travel around the Sun on their long, curved paths. The four closest, Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, are small and rocky.
Mercury is a small world, burned by the Sun on one side and frozen on the other. Venus is wrapped in thick clouds, and at about 465 degrees it is the hottest planet of all.
Mars is a cold, dry world covered in red dust. Long ago it had rivers and lakes, and robot rovers are exploring it today.
Between Mars and Jupiter lies the asteroid belt, a wide ring of rocky leftovers from the time the planets were made. The rocks are far apart, so spacecraft can pass through it safely.
Jupiter is the biggest planet in the solar system, and it is made mostly of gas. Its Great Red Spot is a storm that has raged for hundreds of years and is larger than the Earth.
Saturn is famous for its bright rings, which are made of billions of pieces of ice and rock. It is so light for its size that it would float on water, if you could find a bath big enough.
Uranus and Neptune are cold blue worlds, very far from the Sun. Neptune was found in 1846 by using mathematics, because the orbit of Uranus showed that something was pulling on it.
Far beyond Neptune lie small icy worlds such as Pluto, and many comets. A comet is a dirty snowball, and its tail always points away from the Sun, as Halley's Comet shows every 76 years.

Voyager 1 was launched in 1977, and it is now the farthest human-made object, more than twenty billion kilometres away. Even so, its light-signals take almost a whole day to reach us, and it has hardly left our own small corner of space.
Look closely and you will see that stars have different colours. The hottest burn blue, the Sun is yellow-white, and the coolest glow a deep red.
The pale band across the sky is our own galaxy, the Milky Way, seen from the inside. It is made of at least a hundred billion stars, far too many for the eye to separate.
Seen from above, the Milky Way would look like a flat spiral about 100,000 light-years across. The Sun sits in the quiet outer part, about 26,000 light-years from the centre.
Like everything else in the galaxy, the Sun is in motion. It travels around the galactic centre, and one full circle takes about 230 million years.
New stars are being born at this very moment, inside great clouds of gas and dust called nebulae. The Orion Nebula, about 1,300 light-years away, looks like a faint fuzzy patch to the naked eye.
Stars come in very different sizes, and some are huge. A red giant such as Betelgeuse could swallow the inner planets, but about three stars in four are small, dim red dwarfs.
From a dark place, you can see a faint smudge of light in Andromeda. It is another great galaxy, and the light reaching you tonight left it about two and a half million years ago.
Galaxies come in different shapes: spirals, smooth balls and ragged clouds. The Milky Way and Andromeda belong to a small family called the Local Group, which also has dozens of smaller galaxies.
In 1995 the Hubble Space Telescope stared for ten days at a patch of sky as small as a grain of sand. The patch looked empty, but the picture showed about 3,000 galaxies.

On the largest scale, galaxies are not spread out evenly across the universe. They gather in clusters and long threads that form a kind of web, and between the threads lie huge empty regions called voids.
For thousands of years, people watched the sky closely because their lives depended on it. The Sun and the stars told them when to plant their crops and when it was safe to sail.
The ancient Greeks worked out that the Earth is round. In a lunar eclipse its shadow on the Moon is always curved, and a ship sailing away disappears bottom first.

Around 240 BC, a Greek scholar named Eratosthenes compared the shadows of sticks in two faraway cities. From the difference he calculated the size of the Earth, and his answer was close to the true one.
About 150 AD, a scholar named Ptolemy described a system with the Earth at the centre. He used circles on circles to predict where the planets would be, and the system was used for about 1,400 years.

An Earth-centred universe felt natural, because the ground under your feet does not seem to move. One Greek thinker, Aristarchus, had suggested around 270 BC that the Sun was at the centre, but hardly anyone agreed with him.
There was one great puzzle about the planets that nobody could solve. Every so often, a planet seems to stop and move backwards for a few weeks, and only more and more circles could explain this.

In 1543, a Polish astronomer named Copernicus published a book that put the Sun at the centre. The Earth, he said, spins once a day and travels around the Sun once a year, and this explained the backward loops very simply.

A Danish astronomer named Tycho Brahe measured the positions of the planets very carefully, using only his eyes. Using these numbers, Johannes Kepler showed in 1609 that the planets move on ovals, not on perfect circles.
In 1610, Galileo built a telescope and turned it on the planet Jupiter. He saw four small moons circling it, which proved that not everything in the sky goes around the Earth.

Galileo also saw that Venus shows phases like the Moon, which fits a Sun-centred system. In 1633, however, the Church made him take back his claim, and he spent the rest of his life under house arrest.
In the late 1600s, Isaac Newton asked a simple question. Why does an apple fall to the ground, while the Moon stays up in the sky?
Newton imagined a cannon on a very high mountain. If the ball were fired fast enough, it would keep falling but never land, and it would circle the Earth like the Moon.
In 1687, Newton published his famous law of gravity in a great book. Every object pulls on every other object, and the pull is stronger for heavier things but weaker when the distance grows.
Edmond Halley used Newton's law to predict that a bright comet would come back in 1758. He did not live to see it, but the comet returned right on time.
There was only one small puzzle left in the whole of the sky. The orbit of the planet Mercury turns by a tiny amount more than Newton's law says it should, and for decades nobody could explain why.
In 1905, Albert Einstein showed that light has the same speed for everybody, however they are moving. Strangely, this means that time itself runs more slowly for something that moves very fast.
In 1915, Einstein said that anything with mass bends space and time, like a heavy ball on a blanket. Other things follow the curves, and this idea explained the odd orbit of Mercury exactly.

In 1919, during a total eclipse of the Sun, Arthur Eddington and his team photographed stars near the dark Sun. The light of the stars had bent a little as it passed it, just as Einstein had predicted, and the news made him famous.
A heavy galaxy can bend the light that passes it, like a giant glass lens. Telescopes show faraway galaxies stretched into bright arcs and rings by the gravity of the ones in front.

Gravity changes the pace of time, and clocks run slightly faster high above the Earth. The satellites that guide your phone must correct for this, or their errors would grow to kilometres in a single day.
A star is a balance between gravity, which pulls inwards, and heat, which pushes outwards. When a very heavy star runs out of fuel, gravity wins, and the core falls in on itself.

To escape from the Earth, a rocket must travel at about eleven kilometres a second. On a heavier world the speed needed would be greater, and on a heavy enough one it would be greater than the speed of light.
A black hole forms when a huge amount of matter is squeezed into a very small space. If the Sun could be squeezed that way, it would be only about six kilometres across.
The edge of a black hole is called the event horizon. It is not a solid surface, but a point of no return, and anything that crosses it, even light, can never come back out.
We cannot see a black hole itself, but we can see its effects. Gas spiralling into it grows so hot that it glows with X-rays, and this is how the black hole called Cygnus X-1 was found.
Black holes are not cosmic vacuum cleaners, as films suggest. If the Sun became a black hole, the Earth would keep circling it exactly as before, though in the dark.
At the centre of the Milky Way sits a huge black hole, about four million times heavier than the Sun. Astronomers proved it by watching stars race around an invisible point for many years.
In 2019, a network of radio dishes all over the Earth made the first picture of a black hole's shadow. The black hole lies in a galaxy called Messier 87, about 55 million light-years away.
Gravity also slows down time near a black hole, as it does everywhere. A faraway watcher would see a falling clock tick more slowly and fade, but to the clock everything would feel normal.

Nobody knows what happens at the very centre of a black hole, because our best theories give nonsense there. Theory also suggests that black holes very slowly lose energy, but this has never been seen.
Until the 1920s, many astronomers thought that the Milky Way was the whole universe. They believed that the fuzzy spirals seen in their telescopes were small clouds inside it.

Around 1912, an astronomer named Henrietta Leavitt studied thousands of photographs of stars. She found that some pulsing stars, called Cepheids, flash more slowly when they are brighter, and this gave astronomers a way to measure distance.
In 1924, Edwin Hubble found a pulsing star in the Andromeda smudge and measured its distance. It lay far outside the Milky Way, so Andromeda had to be a galaxy of its own.

When an ambulance speeds away from you, its siren drops in pitch, because the sound waves are stretched. In the same way, the light from something moving away is stretched towards red, which is called redshift.
In 1929, Hubble showed that the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away from us. The Belgian priest and physicist Georges Lemaître had already worked this out from theory in 1927.
The galaxies are not flying through space like bullets. Instead, space itself is stretching, like dough with raisins in it, so that every raisin moves away from every other raisin.
This expansion has no centre, and no galaxy is in the middle of it. From any galaxy the others seem to move away, as dots on a balloon do when it is blown up.

Einstein had believed that the universe is not changing, and he had added an extra term to his equations to keep it still. When the expansion was found, he dropped it, and the story goes that he called it his biggest mistake.

Things that are held together do not expand, so your body, the Earth and the Milky Way stay the same size. Only the great gaps between distant groups of galaxies grow, and Andromeda is even moving towards us.

Today we know that a galaxy moves away about twenty kilometres a second faster for each extra million light-years. However, two different ways of measuring this give slightly different answers, and nobody yet knows why.
Imagine running the film of the universe backwards in time. If space is expanding now, then long ago everything was closer and hotter, and nearly fourteen billion years ago it was extremely dense.
The Big Bang was not an explosion at one place in empty space. Space itself began to expand everywhere at once, so there is no centre, and there is no outside.
The name Big Bang came from the astronomer Fred Hoyle in a radio talk in 1949. He preferred a different idea, in which the universe never changes, but his name for the rival idea stuck.
Physics can follow the story back to a tiny fraction of a second after the beginning. The very first moment is unknown, because our present theories cannot describe conditions so extreme.
One leading idea is called inflation, and it has not been proved. In a tiny fraction of a second the universe may have grown enormously, which would explain why it is so smooth.

At first it was too hot for anything as large as the core of an atom to exist. The universe was a soup of tiny particles called quarks, and after about a millionth of a second they joined into protons and neutrons.
Every kind of particle has an opposite, called antimatter, and when the two meet, both are destroyed. A tiny surplus of matter, about one part in a billion, survived, and nobody knows why.
Within the first few minutes, the universe was hotter than the centre of a star. Protons and neutrons joined together to make the cores of helium atoms, together with a little lithium.
The result was about three quarters hydrogen and one quarter helium, by mass. Scientists calculated this mix in the 1940s, and it is exactly what the oldest clouds of gas show today.

All the pushes and pulls in nature come from just four forces. Gravity is by far the weakest, and a small magnet can lift a paper clip against the pull of the whole Earth.

Nobody yet knows what dark matter is really made of. Detectors deep underground have waited for years without catching a single particle, and a few scientists try to change gravity instead.
Computer simulations that include dark matter grow a cosmic web just like the real one. It seems that dark matter was the invisible scaffolding on which the galaxies were built.

Some speculative ideas say that our universe bounced out of an earlier one, or that universes pass through endless cycles. None of these ideas has been tested, and each could turn out to be wrong.
We can see only the part of the universe whose light has had time to reach us. That region is about 93 billion light-years across today, because space has stretched while the light was travelling.
Nobody knows what lies beyond the part we can see. Measurements show that space is flat, to within a small error, which fits an endless universe, but it does not prove that it is one.

We live very early in the history of the universe. The age of stars will last for about a hundred trillion years, and less than one hundredth of one per cent has passed.
A telescope is like a bucket for catching light from far away. The bigger its mirror, the more faint light it collects, and the Hubble Space Telescope sees clearly above the air.
