It was wrong, but it was wrong in a clever and careful way, and it kept astronomers busy for centuries.

An Earth that stands still at the centre of everything feels like plain common sense, for we cannot feel the ground move, and every day the Sun and the stars seem to glide across the sky. A Greek thinker named Aristarchus had suggested around 270 BC that the Sun might be the real centre, but few were persuaded, since the idea contradicted what everyone could see and feel. It would need new evidence, and a great deal of courage, before the world could change its mind.

One puzzle never went away: from time to time a planet appears to halt, drift backwards through the stars for several weeks, and then resume its forward path. The Earth-centred system could account for this loop only by piling on yet more circles, until the whole machinery grew heavy and awkward. A simpler explanation was waiting, though it asked people to think about the Earth in a completely new way.

In 1543, Nicolaus Copernicus, a Polish astronomer and churchman, published a book in which the Sun stands at the centre and the Earth is only one of the planets travelling around it. The Earth spins once a day and circles the Sun once a year, and the backward loops of the other planets become an easy illusion, like the way a slower car seems to go backwards when you overtake it. He is said to have received a printed copy of the book only as he lay dying.

The Danish nobleman Tycho Brahe spent years measuring the positions of the planets with larger and more precise instruments than anyone had built before, though he still had no telescope. His assistant Johannes Kepler spent years struggling with these numbers until, in 1609, he showed that the planets travel on ovals called ellipses, moving faster when they are closer to the Sun. The perfect circles that had ruled astronomy for two thousand years were finally gone.

In 1610 Galileo, having built a better telescope of his own, turned it on the planet Jupiter and saw four small points of light beside it, which changed their places from night to night. They were moons circling Jupiter, and their existence showed beyond doubt that not everything in the sky revolves around the Earth. He also saw mountains on the Moon, and the Milky Way dissolved before his eyes into countless faint stars.

Galileo also found that Venus goes through phases, like the Moon, exactly as the Sun-centred system required, and he wrote about this evidence with great vigour and no little pride. This brought him before the Church court called the Inquisition in 1633, where he was compelled to renounce his claim, and he spent the rest of his life confined to his own house. The evidence, however, could not be taken back, and it gradually convinced the world.

According to a famous story, the sight of a falling apple set Isaac Newton thinking, in the 1660s, about a question that nobody had asked properly before. Why should an apple drop to the ground, while the Moon, which is also pulled by the Earth, keeps travelling in its great circle without ever falling down? His answer, which changed science for ever, was that apple and Moon are both obeying the very same pull of gravity.

To explain his idea, Newton imagined a cannon on top of a very tall mountain, firing balls sideways at higher and higher speeds. A fast enough ball would fall continuously towards the ground and yet always miss it, because the curve of the Earth fell away beneath it, and it would circle the planet for ever. That, he realised, is exactly what the Moon is doing, for it is always falling towards the Earth and always missing it.

In 1687 Newton published his great book, the Principia, which set out a law of gravity that applies everywhere in the universe. Every object pulls on every other object, with a force that grows with their weight and shrinks with the distance between them, so that doubling the distance makes the pull four times weaker. The same rule governs a falling apple, the tides of the sea and the orbits of the planets.

Edmond Halley, a friend of Newton, used the new law of gravity to work out that the bright comets seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 were really one comet, circling the Sun again and again. He predicted its return for 1758, and although he had died by then, the comet appeared in the sky exactly as expected, to the delight of astronomers everywhere. Few predictions in the whole history of science have ever been so beautifully and publicly confirmed as this one was.

Newton's law worked so well that it seemed complete, yet one tiny mystery remained. The oval path of Mercury slowly turns around the Sun, and it turns slightly more than Newton's gravity can account for, by an amount that nobody could explain for many decades. Small as it was, the difference was a hairline crack in a magnificent building, and it would not go away.

In 1905 a young patent clerk named Albert Einstein published a theory, now called special relativity, which began from a surprising fact: light has the same speed for everyone, however fast they are moving. From this single idea it follows that time itself passes more slowly for a fast-moving traveller, and that nothing with mass can ever reach the speed of light. It overturned ideas about time and space that had always seemed to be plain common sense, and it was only the beginning.

In 1915 Einstein published his general theory of relativity, which treats gravity not as a pull but as the shape of space and time. A massive object such as the Sun makes a dent in the fabric of space-time, much as a bowling ball would sink into a stretched blanket, and a planet rolling past follows the curve of that dent. As one physicist has put it, matter tells space how to curve, and space tells matter how to move, and the theory also explained the odd orbit of Mercury exactly.

On the day of a total eclipse in 1919, when the Moon hid the glare of the Sun, two expeditions led by Arthur Eddington photographed the stars that appeared close beside it. Their light had been bent by the Sun's gravity, and their positions had shifted by just the amount that Einstein's theory had predicted, which was a result that made newspapers around the world. Overnight, the former patent clerk had become the most famous scientist alive, and a household name across the whole world.

The bending of light turned out to be a powerful tool, for a heavy galaxy or a cluster of galaxies can act as a gigantic lens, focusing the light of things far behind it. Telescopes now show remote galaxies smeared into bright arcs and even complete rings, which astronomers call Einstein rings, and the shape of each one tells us how much mass lies in the lens. Gravity itself, the force that holds the universe together, had unexpectedly become a kind of telescope for studying it.

Gravity really does slow time down, for a clock close to a massive object ticks a little more slowly than one far away from it. The clocks on navigation satellites, high above the Earth, therefore run slightly fast compared with those on the ground, and the system must correct for this or its errors would reach several kilometres in a day. Einstein's strange ideas are working in your pocket right now, every time you ask your phone for directions.

Every star is a balance between two great forces: gravity, which pulls everything inwards, and the heat of the nuclear fires, which pushes outwards. When a very heavy star runs out of fuel, the heat can no longer hold the weight above it, and the core collapses inwards with a speed and violence that are hard to imagine. What it leaves behind can be the strangest and most extreme kind of object that astronomers have ever found in the sky.

To escape from the Earth's pull, a rocket must reach a speed of about eleven kilometres every second, and on a more massive world the necessary speed would be higher still. Imagine an object so heavy and so compact that the speed needed to leave it is greater than the speed of light itself, which nothing can beat. In 1783 an English clergyman named John Michell had already pictured such a thing, and called it a dark star.

A black hole is what remains when a great quantity of matter has been crushed into an astonishingly small space, so that its gravity becomes strong enough to trap everything, even light. The Sun is not heavy enough to end its life like this, but if it could be squeezed into a black hole, the whole thing would measure only about six kilometres across. Nothing else that we know of in the whole universe is so dense, so strange or so completely dark.

The boundary of a black hole is called the event horizon, and it is best understood not as a surface but as a point of no return. Anything that crosses it, whether a spacecraft, a star or a ray of light, is bound to fall inwards for ever, because to climb back out it would need to travel faster than light. A traveller crossing it would, strangely enough, notice nothing special at that very moment, and would feel no wall or barrier.

Because a black hole gives out no light of its own, astronomers find them by their effects on the things nearby. Gas that spirals towards the horizon is squeezed and heated until it glows fiercely with X-rays, and it was this glow that gave away Cygnus X-1, the first strong candidate for a black hole, in the early 1970s. In other cases it is the swift motion of neighbouring stars that reveals a hidden, heavy partner.

In films a black hole reaches out and swallows everything around it, but nature is less dramatic than that. Far from the horizon its gravity is the same as that of any other object of equal mass, so if the Sun were replaced by a black hole, the planets would go on circling it in the same orbits. Only things that come very close to it are ever in any real danger of being swallowed.

Hidden in the heart of the Milky Way, in the direction of the constellation Sagittarius, lies a supermassive black hole about four million times heavier than the Sun. Astronomers proved that it exists by tracking the paths of stars that whirl around an invisible point at tremendous speeds, a project that took more than two decades of patient watching. Most large galaxies, it seems, are built around a giant black hole of this kind.

In 2019 a team using a worldwide network of radio dishes, working together as if they formed one telescope as large as the Earth, produced the first ever picture of a black hole's shadow. It showed a bright ring of glowing gas around a dark centre, and it belongs to a giant black hole in the galaxy Messier 87, about 55 million light-years away. The size and shape of that dark centre matched very closely what Einstein's theory had predicted more than a hundred years before.

Close to a black hole gravity slows the passage of time so strongly that an observer far away would see a falling clock tick more and more slowly, its light growing dimmer and redder until it faded from view. To the traveller inside everything would feel normal, at least until the tides of gravity, which pull harder on the feet than on the head, began to stretch them. Two people can therefore tell quite different stories about the very same fall, and each of them will be telling the truth.

At the very centre of a black hole, our best theory predicts a point of infinite density called a singularity, which really means that the mathematics has broken down and nobody knows what is there. Theory also suggests that black holes should leak a faint glow and so shrink over times far longer than the present age of the universe, though no one has ever managed to observe this effect. The deepest puzzles in science, as so often happens, lie in the place where two great theories meet and fail to agree.

Not much more than a century ago, many astronomers believed that the Milky Way was the entire universe, a single great island of stars in an otherwise empty space. The faint, fuzzy spirals that they could see in their telescopes, they thought, were only small clouds of gas that belonged to it. The question was whether those spirals were near or far, and nobody could tell.

At the Harvard observatory, Henrietta Leavitt spent years examining photographic plates of variable stars, and around 1912 she noticed a pattern in a kind of pulsing star called a Cepheid. The brighter the star really is, the more slowly it pulses, so that the rhythm of its flashes reveals its true brightness, and comparing that with how dim it looks reveals its distance. She had, without knowing how far it would lead, found a measuring stick for the whole of the universe.

In 1924, using the largest telescope in the world, Edwin Hubble spotted a Cepheid star in the Andromeda nebula and applied Leavitt's rule to work out its distance. The answer was far too large for the star to belong to the Milky Way, which proved that Andromeda is a separate galaxy, and that the universe is made of many such islands. In a single stroke, the known universe had become immensely larger than anyone had thought, and full of other galaxies.

When an ambulance races away from you, its siren falls in pitch, because each wave of sound has to travel a little farther than the one before and so is stretched out. Light behaves in the same way, and if a star or a galaxy is moving away from us, its light is stretched towards the red end of the spectrum, an effect called redshift. In the 1910s the astronomer Vesto Slipher had found that the light of most spiral nebulae was shifted to red.

Hubble then put the distances of the galaxies together with their redshifts, and in 1929 he showed a striking pattern: the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it is racing away from us. The Belgian priest and physicist Georges Lemaître had already come to the same conclusion from Einstein's equations in 1927, and had suggested that the whole universe must be expanding. The two lines of evidence agreed, and the idea began to be taken seriously.

Galaxies are not hurtling outwards through a fixed, empty space like fragments from an explosion; it is space itself that is stretching. A good picture is a lump of dough studded with raisins, rising in the oven, in which every raisin is carried away from all the others, and the farther apart two raisins are, the faster they separate. The raisins do not move through the dough at all, for it is the dough itself that carries them apart.

It might seem that if everything is moving apart, then we must be at the centre of the expansion, but the truth is rather different. An observer in any galaxy would see all the others fleeing, in exactly the same way, as dots drawn on a balloon all move apart from one another when it is inflated. The surface of the balloon has no centre, and neither, as far as we can tell, does the universe.

Einstein's own equations had suggested that the universe ought to be either growing or shrinking, which he found hard to believe, so he added an extra term, called the cosmological constant, to hold it still. When the expansion was proved, he removed it again, and according to one account he called the addition the biggest blunder of his career. Ironically, a version of that same term would return to physics many years later.

The stretching of space does not make everything grow, because objects held together by gravity or by the forces between atoms resist it completely. Your body, the Earth, the Sun and the Milky Way all stay exactly the same size, and it is only the immense gaps between distant groups of galaxies that widen. Andromeda, which is quite close in cosmic terms, is in fact moving towards us and will one day collide with the Milky Way.

Today astronomers measure the rate of the expansion with great care, and they find that for every extra million light-years of distance, a galaxy recedes about twenty kilometres a second faster. Yet there is a puzzle, since measurements made from nearby pulsing stars and measurements based on the glow of the early universe give slightly different values, and the disagreement has grown rather than shrunk. It may be a mistake, or it may be a sign of new physics.

Imagine running a film of the whole universe backwards through time, frame after frame, towards the start. Since the galaxies are moving apart today, they must once have been closer together, and the farther back we go, the hotter, denser and more crowded everything becomes. Nearly fourteen billion years ago, so far as our best evidence can tell, the whole of space was in an extraordinarily hot and dense state.

It is easy to picture the Big Bang as a bomb going off at a particular spot, but that is not what the theory says. Space itself began to expand, everywhere at the same time, so that no place in it can be called the centre, and there is no empty outside into which it grew. The Big Bang happened everywhere, and that includes the place where you are sitting now.

The name Big Bang was first used in a radio talk in 1949 by the British astronomer Fred Hoyle, who favoured a rival theory in which the universe has always existed in much the same state. His rival idea was gradually defeated by the evidence, but the catchy name that he gave to the winning one remained, and now everyone uses it. Science does not always choose its words with perfect care, and a joke or a rival's jibe can sometimes become permanent.

Using what we know about matter and energy, physicists can follow the history of the universe back to a tiny fraction of a second after the beginning, and no further. At that point the conditions become so extreme that our present theories stop working, and the very first moment, if there was one, remains a blank on the blackboard. It is honest to say that we do not know what happened at the start.

One leading idea, called inflation, proposes that in the first tiny fraction of a second the universe swelled by an enormous factor, far faster than anything since. This would neatly explain why the universe looks so smooth and even on the largest scales, and why it grew galaxies from tiny seeds, but it remains a leading idea rather than a proven fact. Some of the best physicists in the world are still working hard, with new telescopes, to test whether it is really true.

In its first moments the universe was far too hot for anything as large as the core of an atom to survive, and it was a seething soup of tiny particles called quarks and the gluons that bind them. As the expansion cooled it, after about a millionth of a second, the quarks locked together in threes to make the protons and neutrons from which every atomic nucleus is built. Nothing that we would recognise as matter, and nothing like our familiar world, could exist before this moment had passed.

Every particle has an opposite partner, known as its antiparticle, and when the two meet they annihilate one another in a flash of energy. Early on, matter should have been created in exactly equal amounts to antimatter, and everything would have destroyed everything else, yet a small surplus of about one part in a billion survived, and we are made of it. Why nature favoured matter over antimatter, and by such a tiny margin, is still one of the great unexplained puzzles of physics.

In the first few minutes, while the universe was still hotter than the middle of the Sun, protons and neutrons collided and stuck together, forming the cores of helium atoms and traces of lithium. After about twenty minutes the cosmos had become too cool and thin for this to continue, and the process stopped, with most of the protons left on their own as the cores of hydrogen. It was the first great act of chemistry in the history of the universe, and the whole of it was over in about twenty minutes.

The outcome of those first minutes was a universe made of about three quarters hydrogen and one quarter helium, by mass, with only a trace of anything heavier. Physicists worked out this mixture by calculation in the 1940s, long before it could be measured, and observations of the oldest and purest gas clouds in space now agree with it closely. It is one of the strongest and most convincing pieces of evidence that the Big Bang theory is broadly correct.

After the first few minutes, nothing much seemed to change for a long time, for about 380,000 years in all, during which the universe remained a hot and glowing fog. Light could not travel far, because it was constantly bounced about by free particles, much as sunlight is scattered by the water drops in a thick cloud. The fog would have to clear before the universe could become transparent, and before any light could cross it.

After about 380,000 years the expanding universe had cooled to roughly 3,000 degrees, which is cool enough for electrons to settle onto atomic nuclei and form the first true atoms. Suddenly there were far fewer free particles to scatter the light, the fog thinned and cleared, and a flash of brightness was released that could travel across space without hindrance. It was the moment the universe became transparent, and the light of that moment is still on its way to us today.

That ancient light is still travelling today, almost fourteen billion years later, and it arrives from every direction in the sky at once. As space has expanded, the waves have been stretched from bright visible light into weak microwaves, and they now correspond to a temperature of about 270 degrees below zero. It is the oldest light that we can ever see, the afterglow of the universe's own youth.

In 1964 two radio engineers named Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, working at Bell Laboratories in New Jersey, found a steady hiss in their large horn antenna that they could not get rid of. It came equally from every direction, it did not change with day or night or season, and it remained even after they had carefully cleaned out the droppings left by pigeons that had been nesting inside. They had accidentally discovered the glow of the Big Bang, and they later won the Nobel Prize for it.

On the older kind of television set, the snowy static that appeared when no channel was tuned in was partly made by a very small fraction of the glow from the Big Bang. Many people who were not yet born when the discovery was made have therefore seen, on a sleepy evening, a faint trace of the oldest light in existence. Science and everyday life, it seems, are sometimes much more closely linked than any of us ever stops to notice.

Over the following decades, three satellites named COBE, WMAP and Planck mapped the ancient glow across the whole sky in ever finer detail. They found it astonishingly even, with differences from place to place of only about one part in 100,000, but those faint ripples turned out to be some of the most important marks in the whole of cosmology. In effect, the map is a photograph of the universe as a baby, taken when it was only a few hundred thousand years old.

The faint ripples in the ancient glow were the seeds of everything that came afterwards, because a region that was very slightly denser than average pulled in a little more matter than its neighbours. Over hundreds of millions of years this gravity gradually gathered the gas into the first stars, then into galaxies, and finally into the great clusters and filaments of the cosmic web. Every structure in the universe, from the smallest star to the largest cluster, thus grew from differences that were almost too small to measure.

Once the first glow had faded into the infrared, the universe entered a long period of darkness, since no star had yet been born to light it. For hundreds of millions of years there was only a smooth expanse of hydrogen and helium gas, slowly thickening under the pull of gravity, and astronomers call this empty-seeming period the dark ages. Yet in that darkness the raw material for every future star, planet and living thing was quietly being gathered together by gravity.

A few hundred million years after the beginning, gravity finally squeezed the densest clouds of gas hard enough to ignite the first stars, like lamps being lit one by one in a dark fog. These stars were probably gigantic, blazingly hot and blue-white, and they lived for only a few million years before exploding, which is why no astronomer has yet managed to observe one directly. The long age of darkness was over at last, and from then on the universe would be lit by the fires of stars, with many more to come.

The first stars shone so fiercely that their ultraviolet light tore the electrons from the hydrogen atoms surrounding them, carving clear bubbles into the neutral gas. As more and more stars and young galaxies appeared, the bubbles grew and joined, and over hundreds of millions of years the fog of the early universe was cleared for a second time, in an era called reionisation. By the time this era ended, space had become transparent to ultraviolet light, more or less as it is today, and it has stayed that way ever since.

The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, is built to see in infrared light, which is exactly what the stretched light of the earliest galaxies has become. It has already found galaxies shining from less than 400 million years after the beginning, and some of them appear brighter and larger than most theories had expected, which has set astronomers arguing about how quickly galaxies could really grow. The story of the first stars and galaxies, once only a matter of theory, is now being written by direct observation, week by week, with each new image.

A star begins life as a cold cloud of gas and dust, drifting through a galaxy, until some disturbance makes part of it denser than the rest. Gravity then takes charge: the cloud collapses, the gas is squeezed into a ball, and the squeezing heats the centre until the young protostar begins to glow. It is a slow process, which can take millions of years, and it is happening in many places in the galaxy even tonight.

When the centre of the collapsing ball has been squeezed to a temperature of about ten million degrees, the hydrogen nuclei there are moving so fast that they can overcome their mutual repulsion and crash together. This process, called nuclear fusion, releases a tremendous amount of energy, and at that moment a true star is born. Gravity, simply by squeezing, has produced a brilliant furnace in the middle of the dark, and the furnace will burn for billions of years.

In the heart of the Sun, four hydrogen nuclei are fused into one helium nucleus, and the new nucleus weighs very slightly less than the four that went into it. The missing mass has been turned into energy, as Einstein's famous equation says it must, and the Sun converts about four million tonnes of its own substance into light and heat every single second. It has been doing this, without a break, for about four and a half billion years.

A star remains the same size for most of its life because two great forces exactly balance: gravity pulls inwards, and the heat of fusion pushes outwards. The light made in the Sun's core, where the temperature is about 15 million degrees, is absorbed and re-emitted countless times on its way outwards, so that it takes many thousands of years to reach the surface. After that long journey out of the Sun, it needs only eight more minutes to cross the gap between the Sun and us.

Strangely, the bigger a star is, the shorter its life, because a heavy star squeezes its core so hard that it burns through its fuel in a few million years. The smallest red dwarfs sip theirs so slowly that they may shine for trillions of years, far longer than the age of the universe, while the Sun lies in the middle, about halfway through a life of ten billion years. In the end, the mass of a star decides almost everything about how it lives and dies.

When a heavy star has used up the hydrogen in its core, it does not simply go out. It begins to fuse helium into carbon and oxygen, then those into heavier elements, building up shells like the layers of an onion, until at last the core is made of iron. Here the process breaks down, because fusing iron takes in energy instead of giving it out, and so the furnace has finally run out of useful fuel.

When the iron core can no longer support the weight above it, it collapses in a fraction of a second, and the rest of the star is blown outwards in a titanic explosion called a supernova. For a few weeks it can outshine an entire galaxy of billions of stars. In the year 1054 Chinese astronomers recorded just such a new star, whose remains are now seen as the glowing Crab Nebula, so the death of a single star can briefly be the brightest thing in the sky.

What is left of the collapsed core may be a neutron star, a ball no larger than a city and yet heavier than the Sun. Matter there is packed so tightly that a single teaspoonful would weigh about two billion tonnes. Some neutron stars spin many times a second, sweeping a beam of radio waves across space like a lighthouse, and these pulsars keep time almost as steadily as the best atomic clocks.

The very heaviest elements, among them gold and platinum, are not made in the ordinary life of a star but in the collisions of two neutron stars, which fling out showers of heavy atoms. In 2017 astronomers detected such a collision both as ripples in space-time and as light, and the light showed signs of just these heavy elements being made. The gold in a wedding ring was almost certainly created in an event of this kind.

Whether by a quiet puffing-off of their outer layers or by a violent explosion, dying stars return their freshly made atoms to the galaxy, enriching the clouds of gas from which the next stars are born. In this way, each generation of stars leaves the universe a little richer in heavy elements, and our Sun, which contains such elements, must be a later generation, built partly from the ashes of earlier stars. In this way, the universe recycles its raw materials again and again, and nothing that a star makes is ever really wasted.

The atoms in your body have a history that is older than the Earth itself. The hydrogen was made in the Big Bang, while the carbon in your cells, the calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood were forged inside stars that died before our Sun was born. Quite literally, you are made of star material, and you carry the ashes of ancient suns around with you.

About 4,600 million years ago, in a quiet corner of the Milky Way, a cloud of gas and dust began to fall in on itself, perhaps nudged by the shock wave of a nearby exploding star. Gravity did the rest, and within a few million years the cloud had become a new star, with the material for a whole family of planets circling it. In this quiet and rather unremarkable way, in a corner of a very ordinary galaxy, our own solar system had begun.

As the cloud collapsed, it began to rotate faster and faster, like a skater pulling in her arms, and it gradually flattened into a spinning disc. At the middle, where the material was thickest, the young Sun ignited, while the leftover gas and dust circled around it in a broad, thin plate. This is why the planets all go around the Sun in much the same plane, and in the same direction.

Within the disc, tiny grains of dust stuck together into pebbles, the pebbles into boulders, and the boulders into small worlds called planetesimals, which attracted still more material. Over tens of millions of years these grew into planets, with small rocky ones near the Sun, where it was too hot for ice. Huge ones of gas formed beyond the frost line, where ice could form and give them more to build on, so the solar system is the product of simple growth repeated billions of times.

The young Earth was a violent and fiery place, kept hot by the energy of the collisions that built it and by the radioactivity of its rocks, so that much of it was melted. In that molten state the heavy iron sank to the centre to form the core, while the lighter rock rose and later hardened into the mantle and the crust. In this way the layered planet that we live on was sorted out, rather as oil rises above water in a jar.

Most scientists believe that the Moon was born in a catastrophe, when a young planet about the size of Mars, now called Theia, struck the infant Earth a glancing blow. The debris thrown into orbit gradually gathered into a single ball, and that ball became the Moon, which explains why its rocks are so similar to those of the Earth's own crust. It is the leading explanation of the Moon's origin, although scientists still argue about some of the details of the impact.

As the young Earth cooled, water vapour condensed and fell as rain for what must have been a very long time, filling the lowest places with the first oceans. Where that water originally came from is still debated, since some of it was probably locked inside the rocks from which the Earth was built, while some may have been delivered later by icy asteroids and comets. We know for certain that the water arrived on our planet, but we do not yet know exactly how or from where it came.

Our Moon is more than a lamp in the night sky, because its gravity pulls the oceans into the daily rise and fall of the tides. It also helps to hold the tilt of the Earth's axis steady, which keeps the seasons gentle over long ages. Nothing about this is permanent, however, since the Moon is slowly drifting away from us by about four centimetres a year, and in the far past it was much closer and looked far larger.

Deep inside the Earth, the slow churning of the liquid iron core generates a magnetic field that reaches far out into space, and it acts as an invisible shield against the stream of charged particles flowing outwards from the Sun. Without this protection the solar wind might gradually have stripped away the atmosphere, as seems to have happened to Mars, which has lost most of its air. In this way, a magnetic field that nobody can see or feel may have been a quiet but powerful guardian of life on our planet.

The Earth orbits in the habitable zone, a band around the Sun where it is neither so hot that the oceans boil away nor so cold that they freeze solid, so that water can remain liquid on the surface. By about four and a half billion years ago, it had oceans, an atmosphere, a protective magnetic field and a large Moon, and the stage was set. Whether life would appear on such a stage, and how, was a different question.

Life appeared on the Earth surprisingly early in its history, within a billion years or so of the planet's birth. The oldest signs, such as layered mounds of rock built up by communities of tiny microbes, are more than 3,500 million years old, and some scientists think there are older traces still. Even the simplest cell is a marvel that copies itself and uses energy, and how it arose from plain chemistry is one of the biggest unanswered questions in all of science.

In 1952 the chemists Stanley Miller and Harold Urey tried an experiment that is still famous, sending electric sparks through a sealed glass flask containing water and the simple gases then thought to have filled the young Earth's air. After only a few days the water contained amino acids, the building blocks from which proteins and living things are made. It did not make life, but it showed that some of the first steps could happen by themselves.

In 1969 a meteorite broke up in the sky and fell in pieces near the town of Murchison in Australia, and when scientists analysed the rock, they found dozens of different amino acids inside it. The rock was about as old as the solar system itself, which suggests that some of the ingredients of life are made in space and may have rained down onto the young planet from above. The raw materials for life, it seems, were not at all hard to find, either on the Earth or elsewhere in the solar system.

Scientists have several rival ideas about where life began, among them warm shallow pools, layers of clay, and hot springs on the sea floor known as hydrothermal vents, which were found in 1977 surrounded by astonishing communities of living things. Each place offers heat, chemicals and energy in a different form, and each has its champions, but the evidence is not yet strong enough to choose between them. The truth may turn out to combine several of these ideas, or to be something that no one has yet thought of.

One popular idea, called the RNA world, points out that RNA can store information like DNA and also speed up reactions like a protein, so it could have done both jobs in the earliest living things. If it came first, bubbles of fat could later have wrapped around it to form the earliest cells. This is a promising picture, but it remains a hypothesis and not a proven fact.

For about two billion years, life on Earth consisted only of tiny single cells, but some of them learned the trick of using sunlight as a source of energy, a process called photosynthesis that releases oxygen as waste. About 2,400 million years ago the oxygen began to build up in the air in what is called the Great Oxidation, an event that was a disaster for many of the earlier microbes. It also made possible, in the end, all of the larger animals that depend on breathing oxygen today, ourselves among them.

Around two billion years ago, a new kind of larger cell appeared, with a nucleus and tiny power stations called mitochondria that may once have been separate bacteria swallowed by a bigger host. Cells of this complex kind learned to team up, and about 600 million years ago the first soft-bodied animals appeared in the seas. It had taken most of the Earth's long history to get as far as this, and the larger animals were still to come.

In 1859 Charles Darwin published his theory that living things change gradually over many generations, because those best suited to their surroundings are the ones that survive and have offspring, a process he called natural selection. Today we know that every living thing, from a mushroom to a whale, uses the same DNA code, which points to a single common ancestor and makes all living things distant cousins. Evidence for this idea has only grown stronger over the years, from fossils, from genetics and from direct observation.

Life on Earth has been shaken many times by catastrophe, and the most famous of them came about 66 million years ago, when an asteroid roughly ten kilometres wide struck the planet and wiped out the dinosaurs, apart from the birds. Small furry animals, the mammals, which had lived in the shadow of the giants for a very long time, suddenly found open ground, and they spread and diversified quickly. Destruction and opportunity, in the long history of life, have very often arrived together and in the same event.

If the whole 4,500 million years of Earth's history were squeezed into a single day, then the first microbes would appear in the early hours, and the dinosaurs would arrive only in the late evening. Our own species, about 300,000 years old, would turn up in the very last six seconds, and everything that we know as written history would fit into a single blink at the end. We are very new arrivals, and yet we are the ones asking all of these questions about where it all came from.

For centuries people had guessed that other stars must have planets, but until 1995 nobody had found a single one around an ordinary star like the Sun. That year two Swiss astronomers, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz, detected a giant planet circling a star called 51 Pegasi by the tiny wobble that it caused, and in 2019 they were awarded a Nobel Prize. The discovery opened up one of the busiest and most exciting fields in the whole of modern astronomy, and thousands of planets followed.

The Kepler space telescope, launched in 2009, stared steadily at about a hundred and fifty thousand stars and watched for the faint, regular dimming that happens when a planet crosses in front of its star, an event called a transit. A dip of only a fraction of one per cent was enough to reveal a world, and in this way the telescope found thousands of them. Finding a planet in this way is rather like noticing the shadow of a small insect as it crosses a very distant and very bright lamp.

More than 5,000 planets circling other stars, known as exoplanets, have now been confirmed, and the number grows every month. From the way in which they were found, astronomers calculate that most stars must have planets of their own, which would mean that our galaxy alone holds many billions of them. Planets, which people once thought might be rare, now seem to be almost as common in the galaxy as the stars themselves.

The new worlds turned out to be far stranger than anyone had expected, for some are gas giants that orbit closer to their stars than Mercury does to the Sun. Others have two suns in their sky, and a very common kind, between the size of the Earth and Neptune, is missing from our own solar system altogether. Our neighbourhood is clearly only one pattern among many, and the universe seems to enjoy variety.

A number of exoplanets orbit within the habitable zone of their stars, where liquid water is possible, among them Proxima b, found in 2016 around our nearest neighbour star. Several of the seven rocky planets circling the small, dim star TRAPPIST-1, about 40 light-years away, also lie in this zone. Yet being in the right zone is only a beginning, for such worlds might lack air or water, and nobody knows yet whether any of them could support life.

When a planet passes in front of its star, a little of the starlight filters through the planet's atmosphere on its way to us, and the gases there leave their fingerprints in the colours of that light. Telescopes such as the James Webb can read these fingerprints, and astronomers hope one day to find a combination of gases that could only be the work of living things. So far, however, no such sign of life has been confirmed on any planet, and the search is only just beginning in earnest.

Closer to home, Mars once held water, and two icy moons, Europa near Jupiter and Enceladus near Saturn, are now known to have oceans of liquid water hiding beneath their frozen crusts. The probe Cassini even flew through the geysers that spray from Enceladus and tasted the water, finding water, salts and simple chemicals, but nothing alive has been found beyond the Earth. These small, cold and distant worlds are therefore among the most promising places for us to look for life next.

In 1960 the astronomer Frank Drake pointed a radio telescope at two nearby stars and listened, and ever since, the search for radio messages from other civilisations, known as SETI, has continued. The nearest thing to a mystery is the Wow signal of 1977, a strong burst of radio waves that lasted 72 seconds and was never detected again, so that nobody knows what produced it. Apart from that single puzzling event, the sky has so far remained completely silent, despite more than sixty years of careful listening.

A famous puzzle, named after the physicist Enrico Fermi, asks that if our galaxy is so old and so full of planets, why have we not met anyone else? Perhaps life is extremely rare, or perhaps it stays small and simple, or perhaps the distances are simply too great for anyone to cross, and the truth is that no one knows which of these answers is right. It is a question that is as much about ourselves as about anyone else out there, and it is hard to avoid whatever the answer may be.

Each of the two Voyager probes, launched in 1977, carries a golden record, a kind of message in a bottle thrown into the cosmic ocean, with greetings in 55 languages, music from many cultures and the everyday sounds of the Earth. The probes will drift among the stars for billions of years, though it is very unlikely that anyone will ever find them. Whether we are alone in the universe remains, for now, one of the greatest open questions.

Every push and pull in nature, from the fall of an apple to the explosion of a star, comes from just four basic forces. Gravity, the one we know best, is by far the weakest of them, as you can see when a small magnet lifts a paper clip against the combined pull of the entire Earth. It dominates the universe only because it always adds up, and never cancels out.

The second force, electromagnetism, is the one behind electricity, magnetism and light, which turned out to be three faces of a single thing. It binds electrons to atomic nuclei and atoms to one another, so that all of chemistry, and therefore all of biology, depends upon it. Radio waves, microwaves, visible light and X-rays are simply the same kind of wave in different sizes, so almost everything that you see and touch is electromagnetism at work.

The last two forces act only over tiny distances, inside the cores of atoms. The strong force holds the protons and neutrons together against the electrical push that would otherwise tear them apart. The weak force is responsible for some kinds of radioactivity and plays an essential part in the fusion that powers the Sun, so that although we never notice either force in daily life, without them there would be no sunshine.

An atom is almost entirely empty space, even though the things made of atoms feel solid. Its core, the nucleus, is about 100,000 times smaller than the atom, so if the atom were a stadium, the nucleus would be a marble in the centre of the pitch, with the electrons flitting about in the distant seats. The solid feel of a table or a chair is only the electrical push of one cloud of electrons against another.

Each proton and neutron is made of three still smaller particles called quarks, held together by the strong force, and there is also a family of ghostly particles, the neutrinos, that scarcely interact with anything. Tens of billions of neutrinos, made in the Sun's core, pass through your thumbnail every second, and almost all of them go through the whole Earth without any effect at all. The smallest things that we know of, it turns out, are also among the strangest and the hardest to picture that nature has to offer.

The quantum story began in 1900, when Max Planck, trying to explain the glow of hot objects, found that he could do so only by assuming that energy is given out in tiny separate packets, which he called quanta. In 1905 Einstein went further and proposed that light itself travels in such packets, now called photons, an idea that was so strange that even Planck doubted it at first. The world, at its smallest scale, is therefore grainy rather than smooth, much like a picture that is made of tiny separate dots.

In a famous experiment, electrons are fired one at a time at a screen with two narrow slits in it. Each electron lands as a single dot, like a particle, yet as thousands of them accumulate, the dots form a pattern of stripes that only waves could make, as though every electron had passed through both slits at once. This strange double nature is one of the great puzzles of the quantum world.

Quantum theory can tell us with great accuracy what will happen to a million electrons, but it cannot say where any single one of them will land, because it deals in chances rather than certainties. This troubled Einstein deeply, and he would never accept that nature at its root should be a game of probability, but experiment after experiment has supported the theory. Our intuition, after all, was built by evolution for a world of footballs and fruit and falling rocks, and not for the world of electrons.

In 1927 the German physicist Werner Heisenberg stated the uncertainty principle, which says that it is impossible to know exactly both where a particle is and how fast it is moving. The more precisely we know the one, the less precisely we can know the other. This is not a failure of our instruments, which could be improved, but a feature of the way the world is built, and nature itself, at the smallest scale, is a little blurred.

However strange it may seem, quantum physics is one of the most successful theories ever devised, and it underlies the lasers, the transistors in every computer, the LED lights and the body scanners that we depend upon. Some of its predictions have been checked to better than ten decimal places, and yet scientists still disagree about what it really means, and several rival interpretations have their supporters. It works wonderfully well in practice, even though no one is yet able to say fully why it works, or what it tells us about reality.

Over the twentieth century, physicists gathered all the known particles, together with three of the four forces, into a single description called the Standard Model. It works with astonishing precision, and its predictions have been confirmed in thousands of experiments, to many decimal places. For a theory that deals with the smallest things there are, it is a monument of human cleverness.

The last missing piece of the Standard Model, the Higgs boson, was found in 2012 at CERN, near Geneva. It turned up in the Large Hadron Collider, a ring-shaped machine 27 kilometres around in which beams of particles are smashed together at nearly the speed of light. The Higgs particle is a sign of an invisible field that fills space and gives the other particles their mass, and finding it confirmed a prediction made almost fifty years before.

Impressive as it is, the Standard Model is not the whole story, for it says nothing about gravity or about the dark matter and dark energy that seem to dominate the universe. Nor can it explain why the early universe held a little more matter than antimatter. It describes only the ordinary matter that makes up about five per cent of the cosmos, and so the map of reality still has some very large blank areas on it.

Our two greatest theories divide the whole world between them, like two kingdoms that share a border. General relativity governs the very large, from planets and stars to galaxies and the expansion of the universe, while quantum physics rules the very small, from atoms to the particles inside them. Each has passed every test that has been set for it so far, and for nearly a century neither has had any need of the other.

The trouble starts when something is both extremely heavy and extremely small, because then gravity and quantum effects both matter at once, and the two theories give answers that cannot be reconciled. This happens at the centre of a black hole and at the very beginning of the universe, which is why those are the places where our understanding fails. Nature has not set the two theories a difficult question: it has set them the same question.

Many physicists dream of a single theory of everything that would unite all the forces of nature, and the particles they act on, in one set of rules. Einstein spent the last thirty years of his life searching for something of the kind, filling notebook after notebook with equations, but he did not find it. The search has gone on ever since his death, with many clever people taking part, and it has not yet ended.

The best-known candidate for a theory of everything is string theory, which proposes that all particles are really tiny strings, each kind being a different note played by the vibration of a string, like the notes of a guitar. The mathematics is beautiful, but it needs extra dimensions of space that are folded too small to see, and so far no experiment has been able to test it. For now it remains a promising idea, but not a confirmed theory of the world.

A rival approach, known as loop quantum gravity, takes a different path and suggests that space itself is not smooth but woven from tiny separate grains, in much the same way as a piece of cloth is woven from threads. This idea, too, is untested, and a number of other proposals compete with both of them, so nobody can say which, if any, will turn out to be right. Honest science sometimes means living for a long time with several possibilities at once, and waiting for the evidence to choose between them.

Testing these ideas is extraordinarily difficult, since the energies required are far beyond those of any machine that we could build, and a collider big enough would have to be larger than the solar system. Physicists therefore look to nature for help, studying black holes, the glow of the early universe and the ripples of space-time, in the hope that the cosmos will offer clues that the laboratory cannot. In this sense the universe itself is the biggest experiment that there is, and it has been running for nearly fourteen billion years.

In 2015 the LIGO detector, whose two arms are each four kilometres long, caught a tiny shudder that proved Einstein right again. It was a gravitational wave, a ripple in space-time sent out when two black holes, each about thirty times heavier than the Sun, merged more than a billion light-years away. The ripple moved the arms of the detector by far less than the width of a proton, and it opened a new way of listening to the universe.

In the 1930s the Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky measured the speeds of galaxies in a large cluster and found that they were moving far too fast. The visible matter in the cluster did not have nearly enough gravity to hold them together, and by rights they should have flown apart long ago. He concluded that something unseen, which he called dark matter, must be adding extra weight, though few people took the idea seriously at the time.

In the 1970s the astronomer Vera Rubin measured how fast the stars at the edge of a spiral galaxy circle its centre. The answer was a surprise, because they move just as fast as those near the middle, instead of more slowly, as the visible matter would predict. The simplest explanation was that every galaxy is wrapped in a vast halo of unseen matter, with far more mass than all of its stars, and her careful work changed astronomy for ever.

The unseen matter has been named dark matter, not because it is black, but because it gives out no light of any kind and reveals itself only through its gravity. The best estimates suggest that there is about five times as much of it as of ordinary matter, so that the stars and planets and people that we know are only a thin sprinkling on top. Most of what holds the galaxies together, then, is something that nobody has ever seen, touched or even properly identified.

Further evidence comes from gravitational lensing and from a famous collision called the Bullet Cluster, in which two great clusters of galaxies passed through each other. The hot gas of each cluster was slowed by the crash, but maps of the lensing show that most of the mass carried straight on, which is exactly what invisible matter that hardly interacts with anything should do. It is very hard to explain this result by changing only the laws of gravity, and many astronomers think it is among the best evidence of all.

What dark matter actually is remains, so far, a complete mystery to everyone, including the scientists who study it every day. Detectors buried deep underground, shielded from every other kind of particle, have waited for years for a single dark matter particle to strike them, and so far none has done so. A few scientists suggest that no such matter exists and that the law of gravity itself should be changed, but most astronomers still prefer the simpler idea of an unseen particle.

When astronomers run computer simulations of the growing universe with dark matter included, a cosmic web of threads and clusters grows on the screen that looks remarkably like the real one. Without dark matter, the ordinary matter would not have been able to clump together quickly enough, in the time available, to form galaxies at all. In this picture, dark matter was the invisible scaffolding on which the whole of the visible universe was built, long ago.

In 1998 two rival teams of astronomers, each measuring the brightness of distant exploding stars called supernovae, reached the same startling result. The explosions were fainter, and therefore farther away, than they should have been, which meant that the expansion of the universe has been speeding up rather than slowing down under gravity. The discovery was so unexpected, and so well checked, that it earned three of the scientists a share of the Nobel Prize in 2011.

The unknown cause of the acceleration has been given the name dark energy, and it is simply a label for our ignorance. The simplest idea is that empty space itself carries a constant energy that pushes outwards, which would bring back the cosmological constant that Einstein had added to his equations and later abandoned. Whether this is really the answer, or whether something stranger is at work, nobody can say for sure at the present time.

Adding up the evidence, ordinary matter, the stuff of stars, planets and people, makes up only about five per cent of the universe. Dark matter accounts for about a quarter, and dark energy for about two thirds, which means that the great majority of the cosmos is made of things we can name but cannot yet explain. That is a humbling thought for a species that is so proud of its science, and it shows how much is still left to discover.

When physicists use quantum theory to estimate the energy of empty space, they get an answer that is too large by an enormous factor, which may be the worst prediction in the history of science. Meanwhile, recent surveys of millions of galaxies hint that dark energy may be changing slowly over time, although this is not settled, and more data are needed before anyone can be sure. The biggest question in the whole of cosmology therefore remains wide open, and the next few years of observation may be decisive.

Did time itself begin with the Big Bang, or did something exist before it? If time began then, then asking what happened before it may be like asking what lies north of the North Pole, a question that sounds sensible but has no answer. Yet some physicists suspect that something did come before, and nobody knows for certain which view is correct.

Several speculative ideas have been proposed to describe what might have come before the Big Bang. In one, our universe bounced out of an earlier one that had shrunk to a tiny size, and in another, universes pass through an endless series of cycles. None of these pictures has been tested, so for now they are best treated as possibilities and not as knowledge.

We can only see those parts of the universe from which light has had time to reach us, and that region, called the observable universe, is about 93 billion light-years across today. That may seem too large for a universe not quite fourteen billion years old, but the answer is that space has been stretching all the while, carrying the most distant objects far beyond where their light first set out. The edge of our sight, in other words, is not an edge of the universe, but only the limit of what we can see from here.

What lies beyond the edge of the observable universe is unknown, but the most natural guess is that it looks much like the part we can see, with more galaxies stretching away. Measurements show that space is flat, to within a small margin of error, which would be consistent with an endless universe, though it cannot prove it, since a very large but finite universe would look flat too. Perhaps we will never be able to know, since the light from those far regions can never reach us, and we can only wonder about them.

Time appears to run only one way, from past to future, and everyday life is full of examples. A hot cup of tea cools towards the temperature of the room but never spontaneously warms itself up again, and a dropped egg never reassembles itself, though the laws of physics for single atoms would allow either to happen. So where, in the end, does the one-way direction of time come from, and why does it exist?

The answer lies in a quantity that physicists call entropy, which is a measure of disorder. For any system there are vastly more messy arrangements than tidy ones, so that things tend to drift towards disorder, just as a deck of shuffled cards almost never comes out in perfect order. The direction in which entropy increases is the direction we call the future, and the second law of thermodynamics says that it never goes the other way in a closed system.

This leaves a deep puzzle, because if entropy has been rising ever since the beginning, then the early universe must have started in an extraordinarily orderly state, one that was very unlikely by any ordinary reckoning. Why the universe began in such a special condition is one of the least understood questions in physics, and it is closely tied to the mystery of why time has a direction at all. In that sense the arrow of time may point all the way back to the Big Bang itself, and to the mystery of how it began.

Time is not the same for everybody, because a clock ticks at a rate that depends on how fast it moves and how deep it sits in a gravitational field. An astronaut in the International Space Station, for instance, ages by a few thousandths of a second less than people on the ground in the course of six months. There is no single universal now that everyone in the universe could agree on, and in this way Einstein's time is personal to each traveller.

In principle, travelling to the future is perfectly allowed, since a traveller who journeys at nearly the speed of light would age slowly and return to find that many years had passed on the Earth. Travelling into the past is a very different matter, for no one has found a way to do it, and it would produce paradoxes, such as meeting your own grandparents before your parents were born. The future, it seems, is the only direction that is open to us, and even that would be a one-way trip.

Some physicists have wondered whether our universe is only one of a vast number of universes, together forming a multiverse in which the laws and constants of nature might vary from one bubble to another. This is an intriguing idea, because it might explain why our own universe seems so well suited to life, but it remains speculation, and nobody has yet found a way to test it. Science, in the end, can only properly deal with what it can in principle observe, and so the multiverse remains an open question.

The Sun is not a constant lamp, for it grows steadily brighter as it ages, by about ten per cent in every billion years. In perhaps a billion years the Earth will probably be so warm that its oceans begin to evaporate, long before the Sun itself changes in any dramatic way. That is a very long time away, and by then life on Earth may have changed beyond all recognition.

In about five billion years the Sun will have used up the hydrogen in its core, and the star will begin to swell, as its outer layers expand and cool and turn red. It will become a red giant, hundreds of times wider than it is today, swallowing Mercury and Venus and perhaps the Earth as well, though scientists are not sure about the Earth. Either way, the Earth will long since have become a place where nothing at all could live, and its oceans will be gone.

After its red giant stage the Sun will puff off its outer layers into space, forming a delicate glowing shell that astronomers call a planetary nebula, though it has nothing to do with planets. What remains at the centre is a white dwarf, a hot ember about the size of the Earth that has no more fuel and simply cools, over trillions of years, until it is cold and dark. This quiet fate awaits nearly every star in the galaxy, since only the very heaviest stars end in a great explosion instead.

The Andromeda galaxy is falling towards the Milky Way, and the two may merge into a single larger galaxy in about five billion years, although a recent study suggests that this is much less certain than astronomers once believed. If it happens, the encounter will be gentle for the stars themselves, since they are so widely spaced that very few, if any, will ever actually collide. Space inside a galaxy is, after all, almost entirely empty, and the merger would be more like two clouds drifting together.

Today stars form at a much slower rate than they did billions of years ago, because the galaxies are using up the gas from which new stars are made. The slow red dwarfs will last longest, but after something like a hundred trillion years even the last of them will have run out of fuel and gone dark, and the age of stars will be over. Seen against that vast span of time, we live, it seems, very near the beginning of the age of stars.

If dark energy keeps acting as it does today, the expansion will carry the distant galaxies away faster and faster, until their light can never reach us, and one by one they will vanish from the sky. In a hundred billion years or more, astronomers will be able to see nothing but our own merged group of galaxies, and they may have no way of discovering that the Big Bang ever happened. Astronomers of that distant future could be left with a lonely and rather misleading sky, and with no evidence for the great story that we know.

The dead stars will keep cooling, and the white dwarfs and neutron stars will become cold lumps of matter, drifting through the darkness. Black holes will outlast them all, but theory predicts that even they should slowly leak away their energy and eventually vanish, over times as long as a one followed by a hundred zeros in years. These are predictions that follow from our best theories, but they are far beyond anything that anyone could ever check directly.

The leading candidate for the end of the universe is called the Big Freeze, or heat death, in which space goes on expanding for ever and everything gradually cools and spreads out. Eventually all the available energy would be evenly spread, and nothing more could happen, so that the universe becomes a cold, dark and almost empty place with no stars and no change. It is not a violent or sudden end at all, but a very long and quiet one, and there would be no one left to see it.

Other endings have been suggested, though none is favoured by the present evidence, and each of them would be much more dramatic. A Big Crunch would need the expansion to reverse and the universe to collapse, while a Big Rip would need dark energy to grow stronger and stronger until it tore everything apart. Which of these futures awaits us, if any, depends largely on the unknown nature of dark energy.

Looking at the whole span of the future, we live remarkably early, in the first moments of the age of stars, which is likely to last about a hundred trillion years. The universe is today only about fourteen billion years old, so less than one hundredth of one per cent of that long story has been told, and almost all of it lies ahead. The universe is still very young, and perhaps in some ways so are we.

A telescope is, in effect, a bucket for catching light, and the larger its mirror, the more of the faint light from distant objects it can collect and focus. The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, orbits above the Earth's blurring atmosphere and has been sending back sharp images for more than thirty years. Each new generation of telescopes has shown us things that earlier ones could not even hint at.

Visible light is only one kind of electromagnetic wave, and astronomers now use telescopes for radio waves, infrared, X-rays and gamma rays as well, because each kind reveals something that the others hide. Cool dust glows in the infrared, hot gas around black holes shines in X-rays, and the vast FAST radio dish in China, 500 metres wide, listens to cold hydrogen and to spinning neutron stars. Using them all together is like hearing a whole orchestra instead of a single instrument.

When starlight is spread into a rainbow by a prism or a grating, it is crossed by dark lines, and each chemical element leaves its own pattern of lines, like a fingerprint. In this way astronomers can tell what distant stars are made of, how hot they are and how fast they are moving. In 1868 they even found a new element, helium, in the Sun's light, long before anyone discovered it on the Earth, so we know the chemistry of stars that no spacecraft will ever visit.

Measuring distances in space is a job that is done step by step, like climbing a ladder. The nearest stars appear to shift against the background as the Earth moves around the Sun, a method first used successfully in 1838. This calibrates the brightness of pulsing stars, which in turn calibrate exploding stars that can be seen across billions of light-years, and each rung is checked against the one below it.

The Gaia satellite has spent years measuring the positions, distances and movements of nearly two billion stars with extraordinary precision, which is only about one in a hundred of the stars in the Milky Way. The result is a three-dimensional map of a large part of our galaxy, and it has already shown how stars move in streams, where old collisions with other galaxies have left their marks. In effect, it is like a census of a very large city, which counts and locates each of the people who live in it.

Neutrinos can pass through the whole Earth with hardly any effect, so detectors that catch them have to be enormous, and they are buried deep underground to shield them from other particles. In 1987 several of them recorded a burst of neutrinos, a few hours before astronomers saw the light of a supernova in a nearby galaxy, a perfect confirmation of what theory had said. Those few ghostly particles gave us our first direct glimpse into the heart of an exploding star, and they confirmed the theory.

Supercomputers can now grow entire virtual universes from the first moments, following the pull of gravity on the dark matter and the behaviour of the gas. Astronomers then compare the results of these models with real surveys of the sky. When the model and the real thing look alike, the ideas behind the model gain support, and when they differ, they point to something that is missing, so the computer becomes a kind of laboratory for the whole cosmos.

Science advances by guessing, testing and discarding ideas that fail, and the process is more honest than it sounds. For years astronomers argued about whether the universe began in a Big Bang or had always been much the same, as the Steady State idea proposed. The faint glow discovered in 1965 settled the matter, because the older theory had no way of accounting for it, and a good idea is one that could be proved wrong but has so far survived every test.

Science is certainly not free from error, but it has ways of finding it. In 2011 an experiment appeared to show neutrinos travelling faster than light, a result that would have overturned Einstein, but when the team searched for faults, they found a loose cable that was affecting the timing, and they withdrew their claim. That honesty is the very reason why scientific knowledge becomes more trustworthy over time.

Astronomy is one of the few sciences in which an amateur can still make a discovery, and people with ordinary backyard telescopes regularly find comets and exploding stars before the professionals do. Many modern discoveries are also the shared work of thousands of people, some of them studying pictures from space telescopes in their spare time on the internet. No one person could ever have worked out the story of the universe alone.

Here, then, is the whole story of the universe told in a single breath, from the very beginning to this moment. Space began to expand almost fourteen billion years ago, and hydrogen and helium formed in the heat, and gravity then gathered them into stars and galaxies, while the stars forged the heavier elements. Planets condensed from the ashes, life appeared on one of them, and at last that life began to wonder how everything began.

Some parts of the story are as firmly established as anything in science: the expansion of space, the glow left over from the early universe, the mixture of the first elements, and the way that stars shine and die. Other parts remain wide open, such as what, if anything, came before the Big Bang, what dark matter and dark energy are, how life began and how gravity and quantum physics fit together. Good science is careful to keep the two lists honestly apart, and it never pretends that the second list is shorter than it really is.

In 1990, as Voyager 1 was leaving the solar system, it was told to turn its camera around and photograph the planets it had passed. From about six billion kilometres away, the Earth appeared as a pale blue speck smaller than a single pixel, caught in a beam of scattered sunlight. Everyone who has ever lived, and every event in human history, has taken place on that dot, and it is perhaps the best picture that we have of our true size.

In the face of such numbers it is easy to feel completely insignificant, a brief and tiny speck on a planet that is itself a speck. Yet we are the part of the universe that has learned to measure it, to question it and to tell its story, so that in a sense the cosmos is able to look at itself through our eyes. Size, after all, is not the only measure of importance, and a very small light can still be a very bright one.

People in every culture and every age have gazed at the same sky and told stories about where everything came from, and those stories are part of what makes us human. Science does not replace the wonder that inspired them, but it adds one new thing, which is a method for testing ideas against evidence and giving up the ones that fail. What science can answer, and what it cannot, is something each person thinks about in their own way.

The atoms in your body were forged in the same stars as those in every other person, and in every animal, tree and stone on the Earth. All of us share one sky, one fragile planet and one history that stretches back nearly fourteen billion years, and as far as we know, there is nowhere else for us to go. That is a compelling reason to look after this place, and to look after one another.

Nothing in this story has to be taken on trust, because you can look for yourself. With an ordinary pair of binoculars held steady, you can see the four moons of Jupiter that Galileo discovered. On a dark night away from the town lights, the Milky Way and the faint smudge of Andromeda are waiting for you, and the sky is the one great museum that is open to everyone, free of charge.

The next answers may not be far away, for a new generation of instruments is switching on or being built, among them the Vera Rubin Observatory, the Extremely Large Telescope and the LISA detector of gravitational waves in space. Each of them will look at the sky in a new way, and it is almost certain that they will find things that nobody has yet thought of. The history of science suggests that the surprises are usually the best part of the whole adventure.

Slowly the east grows pale, the stars begin to fade one by one, and the Sun climbs over the edge of the hill, its light already eight minutes old. You find that you cannot look at the sunrise, any more than at the night sky, in quite the way you did before, because everything you see now has a history behind it. You gather up your things, and you take one last look around at the hill, the sea of mist and the sky that is turning gold.

You are back on the hilltop, and the sky above you has not changed at all, with its thousands of patient stars and its pale river of the Milky Way. Yet you now know that each point of light has a history, that the atoms in your own hands were forged in such fires, and that every answer we have found has opened a deeper question. The story of everything is not finished, and the next chapter may be written by someone who is just now looking up.
